paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 5.29 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 5 (Part 9)
paragraphs.text: 21 The authorities make clear that, under the Rules of Court, a party may examine a corporate party's employee, “but the evidence so used cannot be read in at trial”. Such statements are admissible only where the statements are admitted or adopted by the corporate representative. The statements are then open to qualification and can be rebutted by viva voce evidence during trial: Esso Resources Canada Ltd v Stearns Catalytic Ltd (1993), 156 AR 178, 20 Alta LR (3d) 327 (ABQB) at paras 4 and 19. 22 These principles are codified in the remainder of r 5.29, which provides that the corporate representative may refuse to acknowledge the evidence of the corporate witness, but is not entitled to refuse to acknowledge the evidence simply because he or she disagrees with it: r 5.29(2). If the corporate representative disbelieves or disagrees with the evidence, he must acknowledge it as information of the corporation and may then qualify the acknowledgement with further evidence. 23 In this case, Ms. Kopala was questioned as a corporate witness, but not as the corporate representative chosen by CIPR; Jurshevski was the corporate representative. He was never asked to acknowledge the evidence given in questioning by Ms. Kopala, never given the opportunity to refuse to acknowledge it, or to acknowledge it with qualifications. To allow Ms. Kopala's evidence to be read in at trial in order to bind the corporate party, CIPR, in these circumstances is a clear breach of rule 5.29. Ms. Kopala's evidence on questioning was inadmissible under the Rules of Court. 24 CDM argues that the court is granted the authority, pursuant to r 5.4(6)(a), to appoint an additional corporate representative if the representative appointed by the corporate party is not suitable. But that is not what was done here; the trial judge was not asked to, and did not, appoint an additional or a substitute corporate representative (we make no comment on whether such an application would have been successful if made at trial). He permitted CDM to read in portions of the questioning transcript of a corporate witness who was not the appointed corporate representative. That is not permitted by the rules. In AMEC Americas Ltd. v. Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co., 2015 ABQB 366, Chief Justice Wittmann interpreted R. 5.29: 24 Accordingly, the interpretation of this Court of ARC 5.29 is as follows. In most cases, an employee or former employee of a corporation who gives evidence on questioning will have that evidence acknowledged as some of the information of the corporation by the corporate representative unless a cogent or compelling reason is stated by the corporate representative other than disbelief or disagreement with the evidence of the person questioned. 25 The acknowledgment that the evidence of the employee or former employee forms some of the information of the corporation is compulsory, pursuant to ARC 5.29(3), when “the corporate representative disbelieves or disagrees with some or all of the evidence of the corporate witness,” unless the evidence is inadmissible. 26 There is no evidence before me that AD's corporate representative “disbelieves or disagrees with some or all of evidence of its witnesses”. Rather, the Category 2 and Category 3 Read Ins are objected to on the basis that the evidence is inadmissible at the trial. 27 There are many authorities with respect to the proper construction of a statute. The leading text in Canada is Sullivan on the Construction of Statutes, 6th ed. by Ruth Sullivan, LexisNexis 2014. In addition, ARC 1.2 defines the purpose of the rules. Also, ARC 1.7 appears to codify contemporary principles of statutory interpretation. 28 Drawing on Canadian jurisprudence, Sullivan describes the tension between the “modern principle” which requires the words in a statute to be read in their entire context against the ordinary meaning or plain meaning of a statute. Sullivan, pp. 16–25. 29 ARC 1.2 has also been the subject of Alberta jurisprudence. The Court of Appeal in Gallant (Litigation Guardian of) v Farries, 2012 ABCA 98 has indicated that the “purposes” provisions in ARC 1.2 change nothing, but may provide some guidelines for interpretation. The caution is that ARC 1.2 cannot be used to override specific provisions on a case by case basis. 30 My interpretation of ARC 5.29 is that it was an attempt to codify the existing jurisprudence, to deal with the vexing and troublesome issues in modern litigation involving corporations, as to the use of questioning, formerly called oral discovery, of a person not selected as the corporate representative to testify on behalf of the corporation. Many previous cases, in fact thwarted a fair and efficient resolution of a matter by, in effect, stymieing a questioner, when the evidence of a key employee or former employee dealt with the very subject matter in dispute, but could not be used in the traditional sense, that is “read in” against the employer corporation, because the corporate representative or officer refused to acknowledge that it was some of the information of the corporation. This in turn lead to gamesmanship in some matters whereby the “ideal” corporate representative selected by a party would be the person with the least personal knowledge. 31 Civil litigation can be difficult enough for the party, the lawyers and the bench without gamesmanship. Modern civil litigation is predicated on full disclosure of relevant and material information on a pre-trial basis under oath or affirmation. Fairness demands transparency, subject to any legitimate claims of privilege. Prior to the inception of the new ARC, the jurisprudence in Alberta had generally developed thus far: 1. For the purpose of reading-in at trial, an answer to a question asked on oral examination for discovery of an employee or former employee of a corporation, the corporate officer must first adopt the evidence of that former employee or employee or acknowledge that the evidence given was some of the information of the corporation: Stearns 1992 at para. 5. 2. An application could be brought where a corporate officer refused to acknowledge that the evidence of an employee or former employee was some of the information of the corporation and subject to certain exceptions that Officer could be ordered to acknowledge that the evidence of the employee or former employee was some of the information of the corporation: Stearns 1992 at para. 10. 3. A limited qualification of the corporate officer's acknowledgment was permitted: Stearns May 10, 1993. 4. A corporate officer was not being asked whether he believed the evidence of the employee or former employee: Stearns 1992 at para. 9. 5. The trial judge would determine the admissibility of the read in of the proposed Read In evidence and would do so, according to the rules of evidence. The proposed evidence must be relevant, based on personal knowledge acquired by the employee in the course of service to the corporation: Stearns, May 20, 1993 at paras 32–34; Holtslag at para. 35. 6. The admissibility of evidence at a trial is ultimately to be determined by the trial judge, not a motions court or chambers justice, in advance of the trial: Wright at para. 14; Holtslag at para. 2. 32 ARC 5.29(1) codifies the law as stated above that the corporate representative must acknowledge that the evidence forms some of the information of the corporation failing which the evidence may not be read in. ARC 5.29(2) also indicates as a matter of codification of the previous law that the corporate representative's disbelief or disagreement with the evidence of the employee or former employee is not a legitimate reason to refuse to acknowledge the evidence as some of the information of the corporation. A reason must be given. And if the reason is given, the corporate representative may refuse to acknowledge some or all of the evidence of the employee or former employee, subject to some exceptions. The rule does not deal with the validity of the reasons for refusal. 33 ARC 5.29(3)(a) is based upon the corporate representative disbelieving or disagreeing with some or all of the evidence of a corporate witness. The only allowable reason according to the rule for refusing to acknowledge the evidence as some of the information of the corporation in the event of disbelief or disagreement is if the evidence is inadmissible under the laws of evidence. In that situation, where the evidence is admissible under the laws of evidence, a qualification may be offered in some limited circumstances. 34 The troublesome aspect of this case is that there is no evidence before me that the corporate representative disbelieved or disagreed with some or all of the evidence of the corporate witness, which on the face of it would trigger the operation of ARC 5.29(3)(a) in terms of the exception allowing a refusal to acknowledge because of the inadmissibility of the proffered evidence. 35 What we have here is a refusal of the acknowledgment, not based on disbelief or disagreement, but simply on the basis that the evidence would be inadmissible at trial. Arguably, ARC 5.29 (3)(a) has not been triggered because there is no evidence of disbelief or disagreement. I am not, however, prepared to accept an argument that ARC 5.29(3)(a) has not been triggered, because “disagreement” is broad enough to encompass the objection to the answers to the Category 2 and Category 3 Read Ins grounded on the premise that those answers are inadmissible evidence. Therefore, I accept that I should determine whether the proffered evidence would be inadmissible under the laws of evidence at the trial. 36 I have concluded that a proper interpretation of ARC 5.29 in the context of the Category 2 and Category 3 Read Ins is that if I could determine, as a Case Management Judge, that the proposed Read Ins were clearly inadmissible at the trial, I may in some cases decide that the corporate officer is not obliged to acknowledge that the evidence is some of the information of the corporation. I am declining to do so in this case because on this record, that issue cannot be decided. 37 Based on Wright and Holtlsag and the preponderance of authority, it is the trial judge who ought to determine the admissibility of trial evidence, absent a clear direction in the ARC, that in civil matters it ought to be done by a Case Management Judge or a judge other than the trial judge. In any event, I find in this case, the applicant has not discharged the onus of satisfying me on a balance of probabilities the proffered Read Ins in either Category 2 or Category 3 are inadmissible at the trial. 38 The context must be determined according to the lessons learned from decades of civil practice in Alberta. For example, when, during a trial, might the proposed Read Ins be actually read in? AMEC is a defendant. AMEC remains a plaintiff by counterclaim only if its summary judgment on the counterclaim is overturned. Even then, the trial judge will decide how the evidence is presented at the trial in terms of the claim and the counterclaim. Conventionally AD will lead its evidence first. In many cases, a defendant does not use the read in mechanism because most of the read in evidence that may have been contemplated by the defendant has already been dealt with during the plaintiff's case by way of cross examination of the plaintiff's witnesses. 2. Guiding Principle to Interpretation of Rule 5.29 In 1400467 Alberta Ltd. v. Adderley, 2014 ABQB 635, 2014 CarswellAlta 1912, Madam Justice Veit said, at paragraphs 29-30: 29 Although it was decided pursuant to previous Rule 214, the guiding principle to interpretation of Rule 5.29 remains that provided by Wachowich, A.C.J. in Esso Resources Can. Ltd.[(1992), 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 309 (Alta. Q.B.)]: 6 I agree with the submission made by plaintiffs' counsel that the information of a corporation is the totality of the knowledge and information of its servants, agents and employees. In this instance, the knowledge of a number of the defendant's employees on matters relevant to the plaintiffs' claims were obtained through the discovery process. The general, although not the inevitable consequence of the defendant's corporate officer reviewing or being advised of this evidence is that it becomes part of the information of the corporation as well. Practically speaking, a corporate officer who has had excerpts from the discovery of employees or former employees of the corporation made available to him will usually be under an obligation to acknowledge that these excerpts form part of the information of the corporation. This practical reality is not equivalent to the defendant's submission that this Court is therefore ordering the corporate officer to answer in a prescribed manner and acting outside its jurisdiction. 7 The corporate officer certainly has the ability to append to this admission a qualification. Such a qualification should have a factual basis and the facts relied upon should be clearly identified by the corporate officer as part of his answer. This is only proper as the officer is under a general duty to disclose to the examining party any inconsistent, contrary or otherwise additional information he has obtained through reasonable inquiry into the matters in issue if requested to do so. At trial, it may be necessary for the corporate party to produce witnesses to support the qualifications to these admissions made by its corporate officer, however this situation is preferable to the alternative previously mentioned where a party adverse in interest is required to call the employees to testify in order to get their discovery evidence before the Court. 8 There may be limited circumstances under which a corporate officer an refuse to accept the employee's evidence as information of the corporation. An example might be a situation where the corporate officer feels the employer did not understand the question asked of him because of difficulties with language comprehension. These situations should arise very infrequently. (Emphasis added) 30 The defendants say that it is virtually impossible to answer the question 27. However, as Wachowich A.C.J. pointed out, there are only limited circumstances in which an employee's evidence can be rejected. The defendants must explain what their reasons are for doing so. 3. Use of Examinations of Employees Examinations of employees may not be read in against the employer. The examinations of present or past employees cannot be read against the party of whom he was an employee, and are therefore for the purpose of discovery only … I suggest that it is one of the purposes of the rules that facts learned upon an examination for discovery of an employee—which as I have pointed out cannot be made use of as evidence against his employer—should in an appropriate case be made the subject of a notice to admit facts. One of the purposes of discovery is to obtain admissions. One of the purposes of a notice to admit facts is to save costs. McLean v. Canadian Pacific Railway (1916), 12 Alta. L.R. 61 at 64-65 (C.A.). While the plain wording of the rule remains the same, the matter of the practical application of the rule has been revisited in a series of rulings in Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. The rulings must be considered in chronological order to understand their collective effect. In Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. (1992), 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 309 (Q.B.), 25 February 1992, Wachowich J. (as he then was) heard an application made on behalf of the plaintiffs for an order which would effectively leave the plaintiff's officer no option but to admit in discovery that that information in the possession of the plaintiff's employees and given by them at discovery was information in the possession of the corporate plaintiff. In granting the application, his Lordship said at pp. 311-12: The two main purposes for examinations for discovery are to obtain discovery or information as to the facts and to obtain admissions which may be used in evidence against a party: McLean v. Canadian Pacific Railway (1916), 10 W.W.R. 949 at 950 (Alta. C.A.). The concern here is with the plaintiffs' ability to obtain admissions from the corporate officer for the defendant. If the corporate officer refuses to acknowledge that excerpts from the discovery of employees and former employees of the defendant constitute information of the defendant, the plaintiffs will be unable to read in this information at trial as an admission under R. 214(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court. Rule 214(1) clearly contemplates that only the evidence of the corporate officer may be read in at trial against the corporate party, not the discovery evidence of the corporation's employees or former employees. The plaintiffs would therefore be left in a situation where the only way they could put the evidence of the defendant's employees given under oath at discovery before the Court would be to call these individuals to testify at trial. This is hardly a satisfactory option as the employees of the defendant are likely to be hostile towards a party adverse in interest to their employer. I agree with the submission made by plaintiffs' counsel that the information of a corporation is the totality of the knowledge and information of its servants, agents and employees. In this instance, the knowledge of a number of the defendant's employees on matters relevant to the plaintiffs' claims was obtained through the discovery process. The general, although not the inevitable consequence of the defendant's corporate officer reviewing or being advised of this evidence is that it becomes part of the information of the corporation as well. Practically speaking, a corporate officer who has had excerpts from the discovery of employees or former employees of the corporation made available to him will usually be under an obligation to acknowledge that those excerpts form part of the information of the corporation. This practical reality is not equivalent to the defendant's submission that this Court is therefore ordering the corporate officer to answer in a prescribed manner and acting outside its jurisdiction. His Lordship then went on and indicated that the corporate officer [representative] could append a qualification to his answers. In that regard, his Lordship said at p. 312: The corporate officer certainly has the ability to append to this admission a qualification. Such a qualification should have a factual basis and the facts relied upon should be clearly identified by the corporate officer as part of his answer. This is only proper as the officer is under a general duty to disclose to the examining party any inconsistent, contrary or otherwise additional information he has obtained through reasonable inquiry into the matters in issue if requested to do so. At trial, it may be necessary for the corporate party to produce witnesses to support the qualifications to these admissions made by its corporate officer, however this situation is preferable to the alternative previously mentioned where a party adverse in interest is required to call the employees to testify in order to get their discovery evidence before the Court. There may be limited circumstances under which a corporate officer can refuse to accept the employee's evidence as information of the corporation. An example might be a situation where the corporate officer feels the employee did not understand the question asked of him because of difficulties with language comprehension. These situations should arise very infrequently. His Lordship then dealt with the effect of such an admission by the corporate representative, at p. 313: Those [admissions] obtained when a corporate officer accepts discovery evidence of employees as information of the corporation are not binding on the corporation, conclusive or incontrovertible. The corporate officer is not being asked to admit the information as true or to say whether or not he believes it and the officer is provided with the opportunity to immediately qualify this admission… It was the matter of the qualifications which the corporate representative could append to his answers which gave rise to the ruling of (29 September 1992), 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 315 (Q.B.). The difficulty was that the corporate representative “insisted on appending qualifications regarding contra-information also in the corporation's knowledge in response to some 200 or more questions as to the corporation's knowledge of the particular information provided by an employee of the corporation.” In other words, when asked if certain information was known to the corporation (because it had been disclosed by an employee during discovery), the representative would agree but then add the other information in the possession of the company. Wachowich J. (as he then was), first noted that his previous ruling had been upheld by the Court of Appeal, (23 March 1992), 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 313. He noted that the applicants were “applying for a further order compelling [the representative] to give direct and responsive answers to the particular questions put to him at his examination for discovery.” In particular, he noted that he was being requested to “clarify the meaning of the qualifications as set out in [his] judgment of [(25 February 1992), 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 309].” His Lordship said at pp. 318-19: I have no doubt that these add-ons, which were appended to direct “yes” or “no” questions, have prevented the plaintiffs from obtaining meaningful admissions from the corporation through the discovery process. Such qualifications in no way fall within the meaning or the intent of this court's earlier direction that qualifications may be appended where they have a factual basis or only in limited situations. I accept the argument submitted by the plaintiffs that to permit the corporate officer to obscure the effect of the unqualified admission by denying belief in the statement or contributing contrary or inconsistent or additional information to water down the admission is to let the officer become the judge and the jury over what evidence may go forth at trial arising through the discovery process. This, in my view, is an abuse of the discovery process and renders futile the discovery process in respect to corporations. I would like to reinforce the point that an admission by a corporation through its officer as to its knowledge of particular information held by one of its employees is not an admission as the truth in substance of that information. Rather, it is the corporation's admission to having knowledge of the existence of such information. At discovery, the examining party is entitled to a direct response to a question as to whether or not the corporation knows of the existence of the information being referred to in the question. If the corporation does have knowledge of information held by one of its employees, it must answer “yes” to a question as to whether or not the corporation admits that such information is within its knowledge. The examining party is entitled to have an affirmation in such a case so as to read the admission in at trial as part of its prima facie case. However, at trial, the defendant corporation as part of its case may call the evidence which is contrary to that information which it was bound to admit at discovery as being within the corporation's knowledge. Therefore, direct response of answers to questions as to whether or not a corporation has knowledge of a particular information provided by an employee of the corporation on discovery will typically require a “yes” or a “no” answer. Any qualifications as to the existence of other contrary information also in the knowledge of the corporation, but which has not been specifically asked about in the examiner's question, can be raised by opposing counsel after the witness has completed his answer to the particular question asked of him and, again, such contrary evidence can be raised at trial as part of the defence. His Lordship then set out the criteria which govern the qualifications that may be made by a witness when asked about information known by a corporation through its employees, at p. 319: (a) The qualification must find its source in some document or an information provided to the officer by someone who can speak to the matter on the basis of personal knowledge. (b) The scope of the qualification must not go beyond a direct answer to the question asked of the employee and must be connected in substance to the admission itself. (c) Qualifications may not be based on the officer's belief as to the true facts or his disbelief of the evidence given by the employee. In the result, his Lordship ordered, at p. 319, that: … the answers of the corporate officer … given at his discovery, which fail to be directly responsive to the questions being asked as a result of the addition of qualifications regarding the corporation's knowledge of contrary information, shall be severed or struck, such that the “yes” or “no” responses are made separate from the qualifications and can thereby be read in at trial as admissions of the corporation without qualifications. Further disputes arose among the parties about the directions given by the court and, on 10 May 1993, Wachowich A.C.J.Q.B. gave the following clarification, 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 320, at p. 324: With respect to the requirement that a qualification must not go beyond a direct answer to the question asked of the employee and be connected in substance to the answer, I make the following comments: The applicant is entitled to put to the respondent's officer excerpts from the discovery of the employees and former employees and in this way can make the respondent corporation admit the employee's memory of the relevant event is part of the information of the corporation. The memories of one employee may conflict with the memory of other employees or that of R. 214 officer or may conflict with other information of the corporation. However, the respondent has not been asked about other information it has from other sources. The respondent has been asked whether the information given by a specific employee in response to a specific question is part of the information of the corporation. The applicant is entitled to a simple direct answer, undiluted with supplementary information or assertions of contrary facts. It is entitled to an answer which it can read in at trial as part of its case. Albeit in a slightly different context the Court of Appeal has given some direction on the questioning of corporate officers on the information of employees in the case of Opron Construction Co. v. Alberta (1989), 71 Alta. L. R. (2d) 28. Justice Côté held it was not permissible for the examining counsel to lump together all the answers of one employee in a question to the officer. In that context he noted the officer may be asked what information the corporation has “from that employee on that question.” At p. 38, in the same vein, if the applicant asked the respondent officer if particular information given by a particular employee is part of the information of the corporation, a direct answer is one which addresses that particular information from that particular employee. His Lordship then went on to comment on the effect of the admission that the information is in the possession of the corporate party. He said at p. 325: The law on that issue in Alberta has been clarified by my colleague Mr. Justice Brennan in Nova, an Alberta Corp. v. Guelph Engineering Co., [1988] 2 W.W.R. 665 at 671 (Q.B.). He stated the information obtained by an officer from an employee and disclosed in discovery is only binding upon the corporation in the sense that it is conclusive proof that the corporation received the information. It is not conclusive proof of the facts related by the employee. Therefore it is not necessary at discovery to adduce evidence to disprove the employee extract. It is the function of the jury or the judge, not the party, to decide what the true facts in dispute are… Clearly, the purpose of examinations for discovery is to discover all the facts within the other parties' knowledge. Consistent with that purpose the corporate officer may advise the examining party that it has contrary, inconsistent or supplemental information and the nature of the evidence which supports that information. The corporate officer is thereby advising the examining party of the case to be met in complying with his general duty to disclose any inconsistent or supplementary information he has obtained through reasonable inquiry, if requested to do so. However, qualifications are separate and distinct from the direct answer required from the officer as to whether or not the corporation knows of the information being referred to in the question. The qualifications should appear separately in the transcript. They must stand alone because they are not binding upon the applicant. The integrity of the discovery process is preserved by permitting qualifying information to be given, typically upon re-examination, but keeping it severed from the admissions which the examining party is entitled to read in at trial. Therefore, in my view, the qualifications, subject to a few that may be raised by counsel that now remain outstanding, should be struck. When the matter of these answers reached the trial (20 May 1993), 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 327 (Q.B.), the question arose as to whether they could be read in as against the corporate party pursuant to R. 214(1). The court permitted the plaintiff to read-in discovery evidence of the representative which contained admissions that the knowledge of the employee was in the possession of the corporation. That evidence could be read-in against the corporation. However, the court noted that the evidence so read-in is rebuttable and is not binding on the corporate party against which it is read. It is respectfully submitted that the key to this ruling is the difference between an “admission” and evidence which is “read-in against” the opposite party. The former may not be contradicted by the party which made the admission; the latter is simply evidence in the trial which may be challenged by the opposing party against whom it is read-in leading other evidence. MacCallum J. said the following at pp. 329-31, 332-33, 335-36: The plaintiffs have applied for an order allowing the use in evidence, as against the defendants, those portions of the Examinations for Discovery of each of the defendants' officers; or the written responses provided by the defendants' officers in lieu of Examinations for Discovery, where those officers admit that portions of the evidence given by employees and former employees of the defendants at their Examinations for Discovery constitutes some of the information of the defendants. For the reasons which follow, the application is allowed. The application is brought pursuant to R. 214(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court… In Alberta, a party may examine a corporate party's employee as distinct from its officer, but the evidence so obtained cannot be read in at trial … The rationale for this is that, although the evidence might be relevant at firsthand, the employee has no mandate to speak for the corporation. What gives rise to the problem here, and in most litigation between corporations, is that the selected officer of the corporation often lacks personal knowledge, and so can contribute little by way of binding admissions which the examiner seeks to elicit. The plaintiff seeks to use as evidence the designated officer's acknowledgment that what the employee said on discovery is some of the information of the corporation, and so get into evidence what the employee said. The argument is this: An employee's knowledge and information is the knowledge and information of the corporation, an impersonal entity who can not think or speak for itself. The selected officer on discovery must obtain and disclose on discovery such knowledge and information which, in the words of the rule, then becomes “any part of the examination of that opposite party” which may be used in evidence against it. The defendant objects on the basis that the employee's statement is hearsay in the officer's mouth; that the plaintiffs are trying to do indirectly what they cannot do directly, namely, read in the employee's discovery. At first blush, there is force in the objection… The parties do not disagree that if the truth of the employee's statement were admitted by the officer at discovery, the statement would be admissible as an admission against the corporation… Returning, therefore, to the defendants' objection, that to permit the read-ins “as being some of the information of the defendant corporation”, would be to permit that which the Appellant Division had prohibited in Dench[Dench v. Albertan Publishing Co., [1931] 2 W.W.R. 116 (Alta. C.A.)]. That case forbade the reading in of employee admissions. That is not what the plaintiffs seek to do here. They want to read in, through an officer, statements of employees as some evidence in the case. These statements would be open to qualification, under R. 214(4), by further read-ins at the request of the defendants. The statements would also be rebuttable by viva voce evidence in the defendant's case… The nature of an admission was discussed by Mr. Justice Sopinka in R. v. Streu (1989), 97 A.R. 356 at 365. I understand him to equate the word admission with the expression of a belief in the truth of the contents of a statement. I think it is essential to distinguish admission in this sense from mere evidence… Mr. Justice Brennan of this Court faced a similar problem in Nova, an Alberta Corp. v. Guelph Engineering Co. (1986), 57 Alta. L.R. (2d) 15 … Nova stands as persuasive authority that an employee statement on discovery, which is admitted by the officer selected to represent the corporation on discovery to be some of the information of the corporation, may be read in through the officer's discovery answers as evidence at trial. The evidence is not conclusive … I agree with the defendants that the scope of examinations at trial is narrower than that for discovery, and that one cannot claim the right to read in at trial everything that has been disclosed at discovery in disregard of the rules of evidence. I further agree with the defendants that we are not dealing with admissions by the defendant corporation whose officer merely agreed at discovery that the employee answers on discovery were “some of the information of Stearns.” Thus, the evidence cannot be read in at trial as an exception to hearsay rule. It gets in because it is not hearsay; but, rather, knowledge of the corporation as expressed under oath by an employee and admitted by an officer to be the information of Stearns. As I read the authorities, there is no binding precedent to prevent the reception of such rebuttable evidence, and there is persuasive authority for allowing it; most notably, the Nova case … Because a corporation has no mind of its own, its evidence must necessarily consist of what its servants, agents, and employees can say. In Alberta, on discovery, and in England, on interrogatory, the selected officer must seek out the knowledge and information of servants, agents, and employees of the corporation obtained in the normal course of their service, and he must disclose the information so obtained. The plaintiffs say that such information may be read in at trial, although it is not binding. They admit that while employees may be examined for informational purposes, their answers may not be read in a trial. The plaintiffs stress the wording of R. 214(1); that is “any part” of the selected officer may be read in. I should not like to leave the impression that one can read these words literally to justify the use at trial of any part of an officer's examination quite apart from consideration of relevance or hearsay. I am dealing here with statements of employees or former employees given under oath on discovery, which, if repeated by them on the stand at trial, would be relevant and would not be hearsay. The ruling I make is confined strictly to that situation. Provided read-ins are held within those parameters, no transgression of the rules of evidence will occur. What I will hear will be firsthand relevant information of the defendant corporation expressed by an employee or former employee through the mouth of the corporation's selected officer. It is, therefore, ordered: (1) That the plaintiffs may use in evidence, during this trial, as against the defendants, those portions of the Examination for Discovery of each of the defendants' officers; or the written responses provided by the defendants' officers in lieu of Examinations for Discovery, where those officers admit that portions of the evidence given by employees and former employees of the defendants at their Examinations for Discovery constitutes some of the information of the defendants. (2) The information so read in shall be both relevant and in the personal knowledge of the employee or former employee. (3) The information so read in shall have been acquired by the employee or former employee in the normal course of service with the corporation. In Holtslag v. Alberta, 2003 ABQB 1028, 2003 CarswellAlta 1794, 349 A.R. 255, 28 Alta. L.R. (4th) 274, Belzil J. reviewed the decisions in Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. (1992), 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 309 (Q.B.); affirmed (1992) 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 313 (C.A.), and stated at p. 277: It has been recognized for many years that a plaintiff may read in, as part of a prima facie case, excerpts from the Examination for Discovery of employees of the defendant provided that the defendant's officer acknowledges that the proposed read-ins constitute “some information of the corporation.” And at p. 281, his Lordship said: The cases referred to do not stand for the proposition that all information in the possession of a corporation automatically qualifies as “some information of the corporation” for the purposes of reading in Examination for Discovery evidence of employees. Discovery evidence of employees is not necessarily admissible at trial. The rules at trial are narrower and the hearsay rule applies. … The case law clearly distinguishes between information which is not hearsay and within the personal knowledge of the employee contrasted to information which is not within the personal knowledge. The latter is not admissible because it is hearsay and does not fall within any of the recognized exceptions to the hearsay rule. In Abramski v. T.D. Waterhouse Canada Inc., 2006 ABQB 942, 2006 CarswellAlta 1778, 410 A.R. 158, Greckol J. had before her an application for an order directing the corporate representative of the defendant T.D. Waterhouse Canada Inc. “to acknowledge that the evidence given by Steven Thornitt on examination for discovery forms part of the information of said corporate defendant.” Mr. Thornitt was a person employed by the defendant's sister corporation, and who Justice Greckol had earlier ruled was a T.D. Waterhouse Canada Inc. employee for the purposes of Rule 200(1). Her Ladyship concluded that the order should not be granted (because Mr. Thornitt “[t]hough employed by the Defendant's sister corporation” was “a third party to this litigation and to the Defendant corporation.” She held that “[h]is statements, elicited in the discovery for the purpose of determining the pleadings, cannot be included in the category of those statements of the Defendant's employees and officers that collectively comprise the knowledge and information of the Defendant T.D. Waterhouse Inc. In the course of her reasons, her Ladyship gave the following summary of the law regarding the acknowledgment by corporate parties of evidence given by employees, and the proper use of that evidence at trial. At pp. 164–168, Greckol J. said: 21 It is true that a corporate party must acknowledge evidence from the examination for discovery of true employees examined pursuant to Rule 200(1)(c) as part of the information of the corporate defendant The issue that arises in this case is whether a corporate party must also acknowledge evidence from the examination for discovery of individuals such as Mr. Thornitt who are found to be “employed” by a corporation within the meaning of Rule 200(1)(c). Mr. Thornitt is not an employee of the corporate Defendant, but rather, is an employee of a sister corporation. The question is whether this principle was intended to sweep so broadly as to capture third parties who have provided services to the corporate Defendant, the confirmation of whose knowledge and information is sought by the Plaintiffs. 22 As argued by the Applicant, the practical effect of a corporate acknowledgement in relation to the evidence of an employee is that the evidence may then be read in at trial by the opposite party. That evidence does not bind the corporation, which may still adduce contrary or supplemental information at trial. If the acknowledgement is not forthcoming or directed, the opposing party is left to call the corporate employee as its own witness, and that employee is likely to be hostile to the party adducing his evidence, or at least will be left open to cross-examination by his own corporate employer. A. — Corporate Acknowledgment of Employee's Discovery Evidence 23 The authorities that hold that a corporate party must acknowledge evidence by the examination for discovery of its employees is found in three decisions given by Wachowich C.J. in the same case of Esso Resources Canada v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. 24 In the first decision reported at (1992), 156 A.R. 161, [1992] A.J. No. 1204 (Q.B.), the plaintiffs sought to compel the corporate officer of the defendant to admit the discovery evidence given by employees and former exployees. Wachowich C.J. explained that a corporation has no personal knowledge or information, rather its knowledge and information is the totality of knowledge and information of its agents, servants, employees and former employees, and there are only limited circumstances under which a corporate officer can refuse to accept an employee's evidence as information of the corporation. While the employee's evidence may form part of the information of the corporation at trial, it is not binding on the corporation, nor is it conclusive or incontrovertible and cannot form the basis of an admission of fact under Rule 230. Wachowich C.J. ordered the defendant's corporate officer to resubmit for examination for discovery on the admissions for information. 25 The plaintiffs then applied for a further order reported at (1992), 156 A.R. 165, [1992] A.J. No. 1205 (Q.B.) compelling the defendant's corporate officer to give direct and responsive answers put to him at the subsequent examination for discovery. The defendant's corporate officer insisted on qualifying his admissions for information at discovery with voluminous amounts of contrary information. Wachowich C.J. re-emphasized that an admission by a corporation through its officer as to the knowledge held by one of its employees is not an admission to the truth in substance of that information, rather it is the corporation's admission to having knowledge of the existence of such information. He held that the examining party is entitled to have an affirmation by the defendant corporation without qualification so that it can be used as an admission at trial as part of the examining party's prima facie case. Once that affirmation has been given, any contra information also in the knowledge of the corporation but which has not been specifically asked about in the examiner's question can be raised by opposing counsel and that contrary information can be raised at trial as part of the defence. 26 In the third decision reported at (1993), 156 A.R. 169, [1993] A.J. No. 1046 (Q.B.), Wachowich C.J. stated that the qualifications to admitting the knowledge of an employee's discovery evidence are separate and distinct from the direct answer required from the defendant's officer. The qualifications should appear separately in the transcript and stand alone because they are not binding upon the examining party at trial. “The integrity of the discovery process is preserved by permitting qualifying information to be given, typically upon re-examination, but keeping it severed from the admissions which the examining party is entitled to read in at trial”: para. 19. 27 Under Rule 214(1), any party to an action may at trial use in evidence as against the opposite party, any examination of the opposite party. Where the opposite party is a corporation, the evidence which may be so used is the examination for discovery of any representative of the corporation selected to submit to examination. 28 The mechanics of the use in evidence, during the trial, as against the opposing party, of portions of the examination for discovery of a corporate officer, or admissions by those officers, concerning evidence given by employees or former employees at their examinations for discovery as constituting some of the information of the corporate party, is carefully considered in MacCallum J.'s decision in the fourth Esso Resources case, reported at (1993), 156 A.R. 178, [1993] A.J. No. 1047 (Q.B.). 29 In this fourth Esso Resources decision, the plaintiffs sought to read in at trial a portion of the corporate officer's discovery evidence which admitted statements made by an employee in his examination for discovery. While the information provided by an employee at an examination for discovery cannot be read in directly at trial, MacCallum J., citing Nova, an Alberta Corp. v. Guelph Engineering Co. (1986), 57 Alta. L.R. (2d) 15 (Q.B.), opined that such information can be read in through an admission given in the examination for discovery of a corporate officer. However, that information must also be within the personal knowledge of the employee gained through the normal course of service with the defendant employer. 30 An employee's statements read-in in this fashion are not inadmissible hearsay but rather knowledge of the corporation as expressed under oath by an employee and admitted by an officer to be the information of the corporation. “The corporate entity is a mere fiction … in other words … the employees and the officers are not third parties but are in fact part of the corporation. The statement of employees are the statements of the corporation, and the issue of hearsay does not arise”: Esso Resources (No. 2), Wachowich C.J. at para. 7. Further, the employee's statements are not being read-in as admissions, but mere evidence that can be rebutted by the defendant corporation. MacCallum J. rejected the submission that the plaintiff must be unable to produce the employee as a witness at trial before they were entitled to read in his or her statements through the officer's discovery evidence. 31 In Holtslag v. Alberta, [2003] A.J. No. 1546, 2003 ABQB 1028, the plaintiffs sought to read in the examination for discovery evidence of provincial Crown employees, including information which may have been received by the employees in the form of externally generated documents or reports. The defendant provincial Crown agreed that the cases cited above allowed the plaintiffs to read in, as part of its prima facie case, the examination for discovery evidence of the employees. However, it argued that the information received by the employees through externally generated documents, although in its possession and disclosed in its Affidavit of Records, was outside the personal knowledge of the employees and could not read in at trial as it was hearsay. 32 Belzil J. stated all information in the possession of a corporation does not automatically qualifies as “some information of the corporation” for the purposes of reading in Examination for Discovery evidence of employees under R. 214: para. 20. A plaintiff may only read in, as part of its prima facie case, evidence from the examinations for discovery of the employees acknowledged to be some information of the defendant corporation, provided that the evidence is within the personal knowledge of the employee and not hearsay, and the information was acquired by the employees in the normal course of service with the defendant. 33 Externally generated records and documents received by employees, even they were determined to have been received in the course of employment with the defendant, does not address the hearsay issue. These documents, although they may comprise “some information” of the defendant corporation, are not equivalent to internally generated documents that are within the personal knowledge of the employees. However, if there is evidence that the defendant corporation recognised, adopted, or acted upon the information as being true, that information may be admitted: para. 30. 34 Belzil J. stressed that while the read in procedure under R. 214 “is intended to create a convenient mechanism to permit an officer whose answers do bind a corporation to adopt as ‘some information of the corporation’ the evidence of employees, … Procedural convenience does not and could not make hearsay, which is inherently unreliable and untrustworthy … worthy of consideration at trial”: paras. 27-28. B. — Corporate Acknowledgement of Discovery Evidence Where Witness “Employed” for purposes of Rule 200(1). 35 The question to be determined in this case is whether or not those principles concerning use of the evidence of employees that is acknowledged to be the information of a corporate party apply to Mr. Thornitt who is not employed by the Defendant, but has been determined to be “employed” for the purposes of Rule 200(1). 36 The answer to this question lies in the purpose for permitting Mr. Thornitt's examination. In my decision requiring Mr. Thornitt to submit to Examination for Discovery, I found that the purpose of such an examination was for disclosure to the Plaintiffs of relevant and material information that could reasonably be expected to help determine one or more issues raised in the pleadings: Only relevant and material questions must be answered on an examination for discovery (Rule 200(1.2)). Relevant and material questions are those for which the answers could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more issues raised in the pleadings, or to ascertain evidence to that affect (Rule 186.1). The liquidation of some of the Securities held in accounts by Mr. MacBeth, on the advice of Mr. Thornitt, occurred before and at the time this lawsuit was commenced in November 2002. Questions concerning Mr. Thornitt's advice about the Securities and their liquidation, and about the results of the liquidation of the Securities are relevant and material questions. The answers could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more issues raised in the pleadings, or to ascertain evidence to that effect. The answers may enlighten the Court as to the suitability of the Securities as investments and as to damages suffered, if any, as a result of the Plaintiffs having acquired the Securities as investments. I conclude that the information Mr. Thornitt has concerning the Securities is relevant and material to the issues raised in the pleadings. To paraphrase the Court of Appeal in Petro-Canada Products at para. 15, permitting examination of this individual, rather than sheltering behind a technical definition of employee, supports the purposes of examination for discovery by disclosing relevant information before trial. VII. — Conclusion 37 The situation before me is not like the cases cited above where the defendant corporation must acknowledge the discovery evidence of its employees as “some information” of the corporation as contemplated by Rule 214. Mr. Thornitt was not being examined for the information of the corporate Defendant, but to elicit relevant and material information that may help define the pleadings. Though employed by the Defendant's sister corporation, Mr. Thornitt is a third party to this litigation and to the Defendant corporation. His statements, elicited in the discovery for the purpose of determining the pleadings, cannot be included in the category of those statements of the Defendant's employees and officers that collectively comprise the knowledge and information of the Defendant TD Waterhouse Inc. In Western Canadian Place Ltd. v. Con-Force Products Ltd. (1996), 39 Alta. L.R. (3d) 432 (Q.B.), McMahon J. addressed the obligation, as opposed to the right, of a witness to provide qualifying information. Specifically, the representative at discovery was asked the following questions (at p. 433): 3. With respect to each passage identified from the evidence of the employee or former employee of Con-Force, is the evidence in the passage all of the information of Con-Force? 4. If, with respect to each passage from the evidence of the employee or former employee of Con-Force, the evidence in the passage is not all of the information of Con-Force, what is the further information of Con-Force which: (a) Finds its source in a document or in information provided to Con-Force by someone who can speak on the basis of personal knowledge; and (b) Does not go beyond the subject of the passage identified? In ruling that such questions were improper, his Lordship said (at pp. 435-36): The real issue then in Esso v. Stearns… was when and how the witness being examined could put on the record qualifying information—that is, facts that were contrary to or inconsistent with the answers already given by the employee or ex-employee. The case did not deal with the obligation—as opposed to the right—of the witness being examined to provide general confirmatory information. In my view, there is no such obligation. A broad request that the officer being examined inform himself and disclose all information on a particular subject and in the corporate party's possession, whether contrary to another employee's answers or not, places an unreasonable burden on the witness. . . . . . An officer has an obligation to respond fully. If, after informing himself, he has information which qualifies his answer—in the sense of being contrary to or inconsistent with the answers already given—then he is obliged, if asked, to give that qualification. If he is not asked for the qualification, then his right to impose that qualification upon his answer is dealt with by the decisions in Esso v. Stearns. I do not mean to say that merely because the answer to a specific question might confirm another answer, such question is improper. To use an example which arose during argument, if employee A has said that the temperature at a given time was 3 degrees; and the officer has said that the company has no contrary information, he can nevertheless be asked specifically whether employee B knew what the temperature was and if so, what he said it was. Here, it is the compendious nature of the demand for all information of the corporate party on each subject matter that is improper. 4. Evidence as to “Belief” Clearly then an officer produced by a corporation for examination may not be asked as to his belief, but I do not understand the Chief Justice to say that an individual party (who has a mind) may not be asked as to his belief in a proper case. On the contrary, he says such a party “might be asked to express a belief.” I hold then that the plaintiff must answer the questions as to his belief or presumption and the grounds of it. If it is hearsay the answer may not be admissible in evidence. Smith v. Conklin & Garrett Ltd., [1942] 3 W.W.R. 612 at 615 (Alta. T.D.).
paragraphs.heading: Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 5 (Part 9)

sentences.text: 21 The authorities make clear that, under the Rules of Court, a party may examine a corporate party's employee, “but the evidence so used cannot be read in at trial”.
Such statements are admissible only where the statements are admitted or adopted by the corporate representative.

The statements are then open to qualification and can be rebutted by viva voce evidence during trial: Esso Resources Canada Ltd v Stearns Catalytic Ltd (1993), 156 AR 178, 20 Alta LR (3d) 327 (ABQB) at paras 4 and 19.

22 These principles are codified in the remainder of r 5.29, which provides that the corporate representative may refuse to acknowledge the evidence of the corporate witness, but is not entitled to refuse to acknowledge the evidence simply because he or she disagrees with it: r 5.29(2).
If the corporate representative disbelieves or disagrees with the evidence, he must acknowledge it as information of the corporation and may then qualify the acknowledgement with further evidence.
23 In this case, Ms.
Kopala was questioned as a corporate witness, but not as the corporate representative chosen by CIPR; Jurshevski was the corporate representative.
He was never asked to acknowledge the evidence given in questioning by Ms.
Kopala, never given the opportunity to refuse to acknowledge it, or to acknowledge it with qualifications.
To allow Ms.
Kopala's evidence to be read in at trial in order to bind the corporate party, CIPR, in these circumstances is a clear breach of rule 5.29.
Ms.
Kopala's evidence on questioning was inadmissible under the Rules of Court.

24 CDM argues that the court is granted the authority, pursuant to r 5.4(6)(a), to appoint an additional corporate representative if the representative appointed by the corporate party is not suitable.

But that is not what was done here; the trial judge was not asked to, and did not, appoint an additional or a substitute corporate representative (we make no comment on whether such an application would have been successful if made at trial).
He permitted CDM to read in portions of the questioning transcript of a corporate witness who was not the appointed corporate representative.
That is not permitted by the rules.
In AMEC Americas Ltd. v.
Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co., 2015 ABQB 366, Chief Justice Wittmann interpreted R.
5.29: 24 Accordingly, the interpretation of this Court of ARC 5.29 is as follows.

In most cases, an employee or former employee of a corporation who gives evidence on questioning will have that evidence acknowledged as some of the information of the corporation by the corporate representative unless a cogent or compelling reason is stated by the corporate representative other than disbelief or disagreement with the evidence of the person questioned.

25 The acknowledgment that the evidence of the employee or former employee forms some of the information of the corporation is compulsory, pursuant to ARC 5.29(3), when “the corporate representative disbelieves or disagrees with some or all of the evidence of the corporate witness,” unless the evidence is inadmissible.
26 There is no evidence before me that AD's corporate representative “disbelieves or disagrees with some or all of evidence of its witnesses”.
Rather, the Category 2 and Category 3 Read Ins are objected to on the basis that the evidence is inadmissible at the trial.
27 There are many authorities with respect to the proper construction of a statute.
The leading text in Canada is Sullivan on the Construction of Statutes, 6th ed. by Ruth Sullivan, LexisNexis 2014.
In addition, ARC 1.2 defines the purpose of the rules.
Also, ARC 1.7 appears to codify contemporary principles of statutory interpretation.

28 Drawing on Canadian jurisprudence, Sullivan describes the tension between the “modern principle” which requires the words in a statute to be read in their entire context against the ordinary meaning or plain meaning of a statute.
Sullivan, pp.
29 ARC 1.2 has also been the subject of Alberta jurisprudence.

The Court of Appeal in Gallant (Litigation Guardian of) v Farries, 2012 ABCA 98 has indicated that the “purposes” provisions in ARC 1.2 change nothing, but may provide some guidelines for interpretation.
The caution is that ARC 1.2 cannot be used to override specific provisions on a case by case basis.

30 My interpretation of ARC 5.29 is that it was an attempt to codify the existing jurisprudence, to deal with the vexing and troublesome issues in modern litigation involving corporations, as to the use of questioning, formerly called oral discovery, of a person not selected as the corporate representative to testify on behalf of the corporation.

Many previous cases, in fact thwarted a fair and efficient resolution of a matter by, in effect, stymieing a questioner, when the evidence of a key employee or former employee dealt with the very subject matter in dispute, but could not be used in the traditional sense, that is “read in” against the employer corporation, because the corporate representative or officer refused to acknowledge that it was some of the information of the corporation.
This in turn lead to gamesmanship in some matters whereby the “ideal” corporate representative selected by a party would be the person with the least personal knowledge.
31 Civil litigation can be difficult enough for the party, the lawyers and the bench without gamesmanship.
Modern civil litigation is predicated on full disclosure of relevant and material information on a pre-trial basis under oath or affirmation.
Fairness demands transparency, subject to any legitimate claims of privilege.
Prior to the inception of the new ARC, the jurisprudence in Alberta had generally developed thus far: 1.

For the purpose of reading-in at trial, an answer to a question asked on oral examination for discovery of an employee or former employee of a corporation, the corporate officer must first adopt the evidence of that former employee or employee or acknowledge that the evidence given was some of the information of the corporation: Stearns 1992 at para.

An application could be brought where a corporate officer refused to acknowledge that the evidence of an employee or former employee was some of the information of the corporation and subject to certain exceptions that Officer could be ordered to acknowledge that the evidence of the employee or former employee was some of the information of the corporation: Stearns 1992 at para.
A limited qualification of the corporate officer's acknowledgment was permitted: Stearns May 10, 1993.
A corporate officer was not being asked whether he believed the evidence of the employee or former employee: Stearns 1992 at para.
The trial judge would determine the admissibility of the read in of the proposed Read In evidence and would do so, according to the rules of evidence.
The proposed evidence must be relevant, based on personal knowledge acquired by the employee in the course of service to the corporation: Stearns, May 20, 1993 at paras 32–34; Holtslag at para.
The admissibility of evidence at a trial is ultimately to be determined by the trial judge, not a motions court or chambers justice, in advance of the trial: Wright at para.
14; Holtslag at para.

32 ARC 5.29(1) codifies the law as stated above that the corporate representative must acknowledge that the evidence forms some of the information of the corporation failing which the evidence may not be read in.

ARC 5.29(2) also indicates as a matter of codification of the previous law that the corporate representative's disbelief or disagreement with the evidence of the employee or former employee is not a legitimate reason to refuse to acknowledge the evidence as some of the information of the corporation.
A reason must be given.
And if the reason is given, the corporate representative may refuse to acknowledge some or all of the evidence of the employee or former employee, subject to some exceptions.
The rule does not deal with the validity of the reasons for refusal.
33 ARC 5.29(3)(a) is based upon the corporate representative disbelieving or disagreeing with some or all of the evidence of a corporate witness.

The only allowable reason according to the rule for refusing to acknowledge the evidence as some of the information of the corporation in the event of disbelief or disagreement is if the evidence is inadmissible under the laws of evidence.
In that situation, where the evidence is admissible under the laws of evidence, a qualification may be offered in some limited circumstances.

34 The troublesome aspect of this case is that there is no evidence before me that the corporate representative disbelieved or disagreed with some or all of the evidence of the corporate witness, which on the face of it would trigger the operation of ARC 5.29(3)(a) in terms of the exception allowing a refusal to acknowledge because of the inadmissibility of the proffered evidence.
35 What we have here is a refusal of the acknowledgment, not based on disbelief or disagreement, but simply on the basis that the evidence would be inadmissible at trial.
Arguably, ARC 5.29 (3)(a) has not been triggered because there is no evidence of disbelief or disagreement.

I am not, however, prepared to accept an argument that ARC 5.29(3)(a) has not been triggered, because “disagreement” is broad enough to encompass the objection to the answers to the Category 2 and Category 3 Read Ins grounded on the premise that those answers are inadmissible evidence.
Therefore, I accept that I should determine whether the proffered evidence would be inadmissible under the laws of evidence at the trial.

36 I have concluded that a proper interpretation of ARC 5.29 in the context of the Category 2 and Category 3 Read Ins is that if I could determine, as a Case Management Judge, that the proposed Read Ins were clearly inadmissible at the trial, I may in some cases decide that the corporate officer is not obliged to acknowledge that the evidence is some of the information of the corporation.
I am declining to do so in this case because on this record, that issue cannot be decided.

37 Based on Wright and Holtlsag and the preponderance of authority, it is the trial judge who ought to determine the admissibility of trial evidence, absent a clear direction in the ARC, that in civil matters it ought to be done by a Case Management Judge or a judge other than the trial judge.

In any event, I find in this case, the applicant has not discharged the onus of satisfying me on a balance of probabilities the proffered Read Ins in either Category 2 or Category 3 are inadmissible at the trial.
38 The context must be determined according to the lessons learned from decades of civil practice in Alberta.
For example, when, during a trial, might the proposed Read Ins be actually read in?
AMEC is a defendant.
AMEC remains a plaintiff by counterclaim only if its summary judgment on the counterclaim is overturned.
Even then, the trial judge will decide how the evidence is presented at the trial in terms of the claim and the counterclaim.
Conventionally AD will lead its evidence first.

In many cases, a defendant does not use the read in mechanism because most of the read in evidence that may have been contemplated by the defendant has already been dealt with during the plaintiff's case by way of cross examination of the plaintiff's witnesses.
Guiding Principle to Interpretation of Rule 5.29 In 1400467 Alberta Ltd. v.

Adderley, 2014 ABQB 635, 2014 CarswellAlta 1912, Madam Justice Veit said, at paragraphs 29-30: 29 Although it was decided pursuant to previous Rule 214, the guiding principle to interpretation of Rule 5.29 remains that provided by Wachowich, A.C.J. in Esso Resources Can.
L.R.
Q.B.)]: 6 I agree with the submission made by plaintiffs' counsel that the information of a corporation is the totality of the knowledge and information of its servants, agents and employees.
In this instance, the knowledge of a number of the defendant's employees on matters relevant to the plaintiffs' claims were obtained through the discovery process.

The general, although not the inevitable consequence of the defendant's corporate officer reviewing or being advised of this evidence is that it becomes part of the information of the corporation as well.

Practically speaking, a corporate officer who has had excerpts from the discovery of employees or former employees of the corporation made available to him will usually be under an obligation to acknowledge that these excerpts form part of the information of the corporation.

This practical reality is not equivalent to the defendant's submission that this Court is therefore ordering the corporate officer to answer in a prescribed manner and acting outside its jurisdiction.
7 The corporate officer certainly has the ability to append to this admission a qualification.
Such a qualification should have a factual basis and the facts relied upon should be clearly identified by the corporate officer as part of his answer.

This is only proper as the officer is under a general duty to disclose to the examining party any inconsistent, contrary or otherwise additional information he has obtained through reasonable inquiry into the matters in issue if requested to do so.

At trial, it may be necessary for the corporate party to produce witnesses to support the qualifications to these admissions made by its corporate officer, however this situation is preferable to the alternative previously mentioned where a party adverse in interest is required to call the employees to testify in order to get their discovery evidence before the Court.
8 There may be limited circumstances under which a corporate officer an refuse to accept the employee's evidence as information of the corporation.
An example might be a situation where the corporate officer feels the employer did not understand the question asked of him because of difficulties with language comprehension.
These situations should arise very infrequently.
(Emphasis added) 30 The defendants say that it is virtually impossible to answer the question 27.
However, as Wachowich A.C.J. pointed out, there are only limited circumstances in which an employee's evidence can be rejected.
The defendants must explain what their reasons are for doing so.
Use of Examinations of Employees Examinations of employees may not be read in against the employer.

The examinations of present or past employees cannot be read against the party of whom he was an employee, and are therefore for the purpose of discovery only … I suggest that it is one of the purposes of the rules that facts learned upon an examination for discovery of an employee—which as I have pointed out cannot be made use of as evidence against his employer—should in an appropriate case be made the subject of a notice to admit facts.
One of the purposes of discovery is to obtain admissions.
One of the purposes of a notice to admit facts is to save costs.
McLean v.
Canadian Pacific Railway (1916), 12 Alta.
L.R.
While the plain wording of the rule remains the same, the matter of the practical application of the rule has been revisited in a series of rulings in Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v.
Stearns Catalytic Ltd.
The rulings must be considered in chronological order to understand their collective effect.
In Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v.
Stearns Catalytic Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 309 (Q.B.), 25 February 1992, Wachowich J.

(as he then was) heard an application made on behalf of the plaintiffs for an order which would effectively leave the plaintiff's officer no option but to admit in discovery that that information in the possession of the plaintiff's employees and given by them at discovery was information in the possession of the corporate plaintiff.
In granting the application, his Lordship said at pp.
311-12: The two main purposes for examinations for discovery are to obtain discovery or information as to the facts and to obtain admissions which may be used in evidence against a party: McLean v.
Canadian Pacific Railway (1916), 10 W.W.R.
949 at 950 (Alta.
The concern here is with the plaintiffs' ability to obtain admissions from the corporate officer for the defendant.

If the corporate officer refuses to acknowledge that excerpts from the discovery of employees and former employees of the defendant constitute information of the defendant, the plaintiffs will be unable to read in this information at trial as an admission under R.
214(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court.

Rule 214(1) clearly contemplates that only the evidence of the corporate officer may be read in at trial against the corporate party, not the discovery evidence of the corporation's employees or former employees.

The plaintiffs would therefore be left in a situation where the only way they could put the evidence of the defendant's employees given under oath at discovery before the Court would be to call these individuals to testify at trial.
This is hardly a satisfactory option as the employees of the defendant are likely to be hostile towards a party adverse in interest to their employer.
I agree with the submission made by plaintiffs' counsel that the information of a corporation is the totality of the knowledge and information of its servants, agents and employees.
In this instance, the knowledge of a number of the defendant's employees on matters relevant to the plaintiffs' claims was obtained through the discovery process.

The general, although not the inevitable consequence of the defendant's corporate officer reviewing or being advised of this evidence is that it becomes part of the information of the corporation as well.

Practically speaking, a corporate officer who has had excerpts from the discovery of employees or former employees of the corporation made available to him will usually be under an obligation to acknowledge that those excerpts form part of the information of the corporation.

This practical reality is not equivalent to the defendant's submission that this Court is therefore ordering the corporate officer to answer in a prescribed manner and acting outside its jurisdiction.
His Lordship then went on and indicated that the corporate officer [representative] could append a qualification to his answers.
In that regard, his Lordship said at p.
312: The corporate officer certainly has the ability to append to this admission a qualification.
Such a qualification should have a factual basis and the facts relied upon should be clearly identified by the corporate officer as part of his answer.

This is only proper as the officer is under a general duty to disclose to the examining party any inconsistent, contrary or otherwise additional information he has obtained through reasonable inquiry into the matters in issue if requested to do so.

At trial, it may be necessary for the corporate party to produce witnesses to support the qualifications to these admissions made by its corporate officer, however this situation is preferable to the alternative previously mentioned where a party adverse in interest is required to call the employees to testify in order to get their discovery evidence before the Court.
There may be limited circumstances under which a corporate officer can refuse to accept the employee's evidence as information of the corporation.
An example might be a situation where the corporate officer feels the employee did not understand the question asked of him because of difficulties with language comprehension.
These situations should arise very infrequently.
His Lordship then dealt with the effect of such an admission by the corporate representative, at p.
313: Those [admissions] obtained when a corporate officer accepts discovery evidence of employees as information of the corporation are not binding on the corporation, conclusive or incontrovertible.

The corporate officer is not being asked to admit the information as true or to say whether or not he believes it and the officer is provided with the opportunity to immediately qualify this admission… It was the matter of the qualifications which the corporate representative could append to his answers which gave rise to the ruling of (29 September 1992), 20 Alta.
L.R.

The difficulty was that the corporate representative “insisted on appending qualifications regarding contra-information also in the corporation's knowledge in response to some 200 or more questions as to the corporation's knowledge of the particular information provided by an employee of the corporation.” In other words, when asked if certain information was known to the corporation (because it had been disclosed by an employee during discovery), the representative would agree but then add the other information in the possession of the company.
Wachowich J.
(as he then was), first noted that his previous ruling had been upheld by the Court of Appeal, (23 March 1992), 20 Alta.
L.R.

He noted that the applicants were “applying for a further order compelling [the representative] to give direct and responsive answers to the particular questions put to him at his examination for discovery.” In particular, he noted that he was being requested to “clarify the meaning of the qualifications as set out in [his] judgment of [(25 February 1992), 20 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 309].” His Lordship said at pp.

318-19: I have no doubt that these add-ons, which were appended to direct “yes” or “no” questions, have prevented the plaintiffs from obtaining meaningful admissions from the corporation through the discovery process.

Such qualifications in no way fall within the meaning or the intent of this court's earlier direction that qualifications may be appended where they have a factual basis or only in limited situations.

I accept the argument submitted by the plaintiffs that to permit the corporate officer to obscure the effect of the unqualified admission by denying belief in the statement or contributing contrary or inconsistent or additional information to water down the admission is to let the officer become the judge and the jury over what evidence may go forth at trial arising through the discovery process.
This, in my view, is an abuse of the discovery process and renders futile the discovery process in respect to corporations.

I would like to reinforce the point that an admission by a corporation through its officer as to its knowledge of particular information held by one of its employees is not an admission as the truth in substance of that information.
Rather, it is the corporation's admission to having knowledge of the existence of such information.
At discovery, the examining party is entitled to a direct response to a question as to whether or not the corporation knows of the existence of the information being referred to in the question.

If the corporation does have knowledge of information held by one of its employees, it must answer “yes” to a question as to whether or not the corporation admits that such information is within its knowledge.
The examining party is entitled to have an affirmation in such a case so as to read the admission in at trial as part of its prima facie case.

However, at trial, the defendant corporation as part of its case may call the evidence which is contrary to that information which it was bound to admit at discovery as being within the corporation's knowledge.

Therefore, direct response of answers to questions as to whether or not a corporation has knowledge of a particular information provided by an employee of the corporation on discovery will typically require a “yes” or a “no” answer.
