paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.31:1 Rule 5.31 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.31. 1. An Overview of “Discovery as Evidence” In Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada, 2002 ABCA 110, 2002 CarswellAlta 603, 303 A.R. 43, 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 1; additional reasons at 2002 ABCA 150, 2002 CarswellAlta 788, 303 A.R. 43 at 61, 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 24, the Court of Appeal gave the following summary of the law as it relates to the use of examinations for discovery as evidence. At pp. 5-6, the Court said: Therefore, the remaining question is what types of discovery material are admissible in evidence, and against whom. Alberta law on that subject is well settled. The Rules of Court are explicit, and have been validated several times by legislation and so have the force of a statute. We will begin with oral discovery (examination for discovery transcripts), and then go on to discovery of records. No one can adduce his or her own answers given on examination for discovery as evidence. All examinations for discovery in Alberta are conducted on that basic understanding. Paquin v. Gainers Inc., [1990] 2 W.W.R. 378, 101 A.R. 290 (C.A.). Sterling Trusts Corp. v. Postma, [1965] S.C.R. 324, 48 D.L.R. (2d) 423, 347 [S.C.R.]. (The only partial exception is connected answers after a read-in by an opposing party, which has not occurred here.) Employees or ex-employees can be examined for discovery, but their answers are not admissible in evidence at all: Pelican Oil & Gas Co. v Northern Alberta Natural Gas & Development Co., [1918] 1 W.W.R. 957, 14 Alta. L.R. 172 (C.A.); McLean v. C.P.R. (No. 1) (1916), 10 W.W.R. 949, 12 Alta. L.R. 61, (C.A.), 951 [W.W.R.]; Empire Financiers v. Nance, [1920] 1 W.W.R. 694, 16 Alta. L.R. 109, (C.A.), 697 [W.W.R.]; Dench v. Albertan Publishing Co., [1931] 2 W.W.R. 116, 25 Alta. L.R. 326 (C.A.), 120 [W.W.R.]. There may be an exception where a party confirms the correctness of such answers, or adopts them as his or her own. No one suggests that that occurred here (with a few minor exceptions). An answer given by a party on examination for discovery is admissible in evidence against that party. But it is inadmissible against any other party, whether on the same side or not: Syncrude Canada Ltd. et al. v. Canadian Bechtel Ltd. et al., [1994] 4 W.W.R. 397, 149 A.R. 54, 63 W.A.C. 54, 16 Alta. L.R. (3d) 153 (C.A.); cf. Paquin v. Gainers, supra. Rule 214(1) makes that plain, and the case law and practice are uniform and undoubted. An officer selected by a corporation for examination for discovery to answer for it is considered to answer for the corporation, and his or her answers are presumed to be its answers: Opron Construction Co. v. Alberta (1990), 100 A.R. 58 (C.A.) …, 63. … Now we turn to discovery of records (sometimes called an affidavit on production). In general, an affidavit of records does not transform any of the records (documents) listed in any of its schedules into evidence. There are only two narrow exceptions, both created by R. 192(1). It deems that both parties (sides) admit that (a) those records “are authentic”, and (b) if copies of letters or messages appear to have been sent, the originals were sent and were received by the addressee. We consider “authentic” to mean that the record is what it purports to be and is not a forgery. It probably also means that if it purports to be a copy, it is an accurate copy. An affidavit of records never makes a record evidence of the truth of its contents. For example, most affidavits of records would list or identify a demand letter by the plaintiff to the defendant. That would be prima facie evidence that demand was made, but it would be no evidence whatever that the demand was well founded, or that any facts alleged in the demand letter were true. Furthermore, there are exceptions to deemed admissions (a) and (b) above. A notice of non-admission may be given (or included in the affidavit of records: R. 192(3)). The party who is deemed to admit authenticity, despatch, and receipt of a message may still object to its admissibility in evidence (R. 192(2)(b)). And the entire rule on these deemed admissions ceases to apply at all, if the pleadings of the party deny the authenticity or receipt or despatch of a record (document) (R. 192(6)). Of course a letter might contain an admission by the author, and so be admissible at common law against him, once there was proof (or deemed proof) of authenticity of the letter. In Strategic Acquistion Corp. v. Multus Investment Corp., 2016 ABQB 681, 2016 CarswellAlta 2386, 45 Alta. L.R. (6th) 102, 73 R.P.R. (5th) 79, the Plaintiff (SAC) questioned, pursuant to Part V of the Rules, a Mr. Wallach (who was a director of “162/Starke” which was one of the defendants). At trial, Mr. Wallach was not called by 162/Starke, but SAC did call him as its own witness, and he was examined-in-chief by SAC. “At the close of trial, SAC sought to read in several passages of the transcript from the Questioning. Starke objected to the admissibility of these read-ins based on SAC's failure to put them to Mr. Wallach during his examination-in-chief” (paragraph 19). Justice Mahoney put the issue in these words: 20 Is SAC entitled to read-in passages of the transcript from the Questioning despite not putting them to Mr. Wallach during his examination-in-chief? His Lordship said: 21 A full analysis of this issue requires an examination of the intended use of the read-ins along with a close reading of the testimony given at trial. The law in this area spans the Rules, the Alberta Evidence Act, RSA 2000, c A-18, and the common law. … 24 Section 22 of the AEA and the oft-cited rule in Browne v Dunn (1893), 6 R 67 (UK HL) are closely related. The Supreme Court of Canada confirmed that the rule in Browne v Dunn applies in Canada: R v Lyttle, 2004 SCC 5, [2004] 1 SCR 193, at paras 64-65. The rule in Browne v Dunn applies in Alberta in the civil context as well: 410675 Alberta Ltd. v Trail South Developments Inc, 2011 ABQB 151, 508 AR 198; Pawlett v Dominion Protection Services Ltd, 2007 ABQB 415, 424 AR 107, rev'd on other grounds 2008 ABCA 369, 440 AR 241 (aff'd on the Browne v Dunn issue); Lindahl Estate v Olsen, 2004 ABQB 191, 359 AR 100. 25 However, section 22 and the rule in Browne v Dunn are not exactly the same. Justice Watson described the difference as follows in Lindahl, at paras 23 and 35-36: It is my view that Section 22 and Section 23 of the Alberta Evidence Act to which reference has been made, are, to some extent, a confirmation of the rule in Browne v. Dunn—which has existed for some time in the common law—and serve other purposes as well, of course. … That still, however, leaves the question of whether or not one has to consider the rule in Browne v. Dunn because the rule in Browne v. Dunn has a certain fairness feature that transcends the actual application of the question of cross-examination on statements under the Alberta Evidence Act. That is because the rule in Browne v. Dunn requires that ordinarily—as a matter of fairness in a criminal or civil trial context—if one is going to put a different version of the events to a witness, one also has to do that in a fair manner as well as putting prior statements to the person. That is one of the reasons why I said the rule in Browne v. Dunn and Section 22 of the Alberta Evidence Act were somewhat different in terms of their scope of application. [Emphasis added.] 26 Following the logic in the preceding passage, it is safe to say that section 22 of the Alberta Evidence Act codifies the rule in Browne v Dunn, but only as it applies to a witness confronted with “previous statements made by the witness in writing, or reduced to writing”. The facts of this case fit squarely within the purview of section 22 as the read-ins are “previous statements made by the witness in writing, or reduced to writing”. Therefore, the cases dealing specifically with read-ins, as opposed to those dealing with the rule in Browne v Dunn generally, will be most applicable to this case. (d)—Analysis Regarding the Admissibility of Read-Ins 27 The analysis regarding the admissibility and weight of read-ins involves the following three steps: (1) categorize each read-in based on its intended use; (2) determine whether counsel has met its obligations based on the categorizations; and (3) determine the appropriate remedy if necessary. For examples of this process, see: Trail South, at paras 22–63; Edmonton (City) v Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc, 2000 ABQB 265, 265 AR 285, at paras 25–36, 40–51, 48–65; and Envision Credit Union v The Queen, 2010 TCC 353, 2010 DTC 1235at paras 22–34. 28 The first step is to categorize each read-in based on how that party intends to use it for its case. In Trail South at para 12, citing Envision, this Court described the ways in which read-ins might be used in a civil trial: I would prefer to characterize the possibilities in relation to the introduction of excerpts from the discovery examination of a witness who has testified during the hearing, as follows: Either: (a) the discovery excerpts deal with matters that were dealt with by the witness during his or her testimony at the hearing; or (b) the discovery excerpts deal with matters that were not dealt with by the witness during his or her testimony at the hearing. If the discovery excerpts deal with matters that were dealt with by the witness during his or her testimony at the hearing, then it seems to me, as noted by the Appellant, that the answers given at discovery would either confirm the evidence of the witness given at the hearing or would contradict or cast doubt on the evidence of the witness given at the hearing. 29 In the current case, 162/Starke submits that SAC implicitly asks this Court to accord more weight to Mr. Wallach's read-ins when they conflict with his trial testimony and asks the Court to ignore instances where SAC's counsel declined to ask Mr. Wallach questions on certain areas and instead rely on read-ins. 162/Starke takes the position that some of SAC's read-ins are contradictory and that others are additive. SAC acknowledges that at least some of its read-ins conflict with Mr. Wallach's testimony at trial and that the conflicting evidence can and should be used to assess credibility. 30 Section 22 of the AEA and the rule in Browne v Dunn are engaged when the read-ins are being introduced to impeach the witness' credibility. Section 22 requires, and the case law confirms, that, “the witness's attention shall, before the contradictory proof is given, be called to those parts of the writing that are to be used for the purpose of contradicting the witness”; Trail South, at para 12; Lovat Tunnel, at paras 29-30. 31 In this case, SAC did not confront Mr. Wallach with any of its proposed read-ins. SAC submits that, “the fact that SAC called Mr. Wallach limited the nature of the questions SAC could ask and left him open to cross-examination by his former corporation. In these circumstances, SAC submits that Mr. Wallach's read-ins … should be admitted.” 32 The AEA provides a procedure for impeaching a witness on both examination-in-chief and cross-examination: ss. 23, 25. In addition, at paragraph 223 of Guarantee Co of North America v Beasse (1992) 124 AR 161 (QB), Justice Rooke stated the following: I am of the opinion that, with respect to challenging the credibility of a witness, the most appropriate procedure is that the witness be challenged on any alleged previous inconsistent statement in cross-examination, when an alleged contradictory statement is referred to in examination-in-chief (as in a hostile witness situation) or in cross-examination …[Emphasis added.] 33 Therefore, to the extent that SAC seeks to introduce read-ins to impeach Mr. Wallach's credibility, it has violated section 22 of the AEA and the rule in Browne v Dunn. Those read-ins are inadmissible. 34 Parties ought not to use read-ins to duplicate what a witness has said on the stand. If the read-in excerpts reflect the same questions that are asked during the hearing and reflect the same answers, then there is no probative value in admitting the excerpts and the excerpts should and will be excluded on the same basis as prior consistent statements: Trail South, at para 12. 35 When dealing with additional (additive) admissions, the cases culminating in Trail South permit the Court to exercise its discretion to allow a party to read-in admissions that a witness did not address in examination-in-chief and are not tendered to impeach credibility. This approach allows for flexibility in appropriate cases and is consistent with the Foundational Rules that mandate for just, fair, timely and inexpensive resolution of claims (Rule 1.1(1)) and using the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense (Rule 1.2(2)(b)). In Reed v. Reed, 2018 ABQB 960, 2018 CarswellAlta 2799 (Master), Master Schlosser discussed the use of Questioning transcripts. The defendants brought an application to dismiss an action, and filed the Questioning transcripts of all of the parties. The learned Master said: [9] A few comments about the evidence are necessary. First of all, the Defendants have filed the Questioning transcripts of all of the parties in support of their applications. They are, of course, permitted to do this for their questioning of the Plaintiff, but, typically, only selected parts of the transcript are put into evidence. When the entire transcript is put in, all of the evidence goes in, and becomes evidence at large. [10] Rule 5.31 of the Alberta Rules of Court provides: (1) Subject to rule 5.29 [Acknowledgment of corporate witness's evidence], a party may use in support of an application or proceeding or at trial as against a party adverse in interest any of the evidence of that other party in a transcript of questioning under rule 5.17 [People who can be questioned] or 5.18 [Persons providing services to a corporation] and any of the evidence in the answers of that other party to written questions under rule 5.28 [Written questions]. (2) Evidence referred to in subrule (1) is evidence only of the questioning party who uses the transcript evidence or the answers to the written questions, and is evidence only against the party who was questioned. (3) If only a portion of a transcript or a portion of the answers to the written questions is used, the Court may, on application, direct that all or each other portion of the transcript or answers also be used if all or any other portion is so connected with the portion used that it would or might be misleading not to use all or any other portion of the transcript or other answers. (Emphasis added) [11] What this means is that you can use evidence and admissions you have obtained against the other side. Ordinarily you cannot use your own evidence by filing your own transcript even if your witness dies (eg Paquin v Gainers Inc, (1989) 1989 CanLII 3204 (AB QB), 98 AR 39 QB, and see Waquan v Canada, 2002 ABCA 110 (CanLII)). [12] It is not like an examination on an affidavit where it all goes in and it is open to both sides to use. [13] The distinction between examination on an affidavit and questioning permits greater latitude at the questioning, and, generally, with impunity. It permits an exploration of the case against you. That is why it used to be known as “discovery” before the rules were improved. [14] In Weatherford Canada Partnership v Addie, 2016 ABQB 188 (CanLII) case, Veit J held: Relying on Rule 5.31(2), Artemis objects to Weatherford's use of portions of Dunn's questioning which have not been included in Artemis' position. Naturally, Weatherford cannot use Dunn's questioning in a self-serving way as, for example, an oath-helping device. On the other hand, Weatherford is entitled to ensure that any excerpt from Dunn's evidence on which the applicants rely constitutes a fair representation of Dunn's evidence. I consider that Weatherford's reliance on additional portions of Dunn's questioning is merely Weatherford's attempt to ensure fair representation of the evidence. [15] Using evidence to qualify or explain does not permit “carte blanche” use of your own transcript. Usually it can only be used in conjunction with evidence that the other side has put in; provided that the Court can be persuaded that the evidence put in by the other side would be misleading or incomplete on its own. [16] I acknowledge that evidence that the parties seek to rely on could be addressed with an affidavit and this procedural issue could be cured. It is a less than desirable practise (used by some) to attach excerpts from a party's own questioning as an exhibit to their affidavit and swear to its truth. The issue here is really a formal one which could easily be corrected on appeal, or on an adjournment for supplementary affidavits. It is important to be pragmatic at applications such as these. However, the questioning for discovery of Ruby Reed and Daniel Reed filed by the Defendants themselves are not admissible in their present form. They have filed their own affidavits and I am not aware of any critical gaps in the evidence that need be filed by resort to these questioning transcripts. So I am not going to look at them. On the other hand, all of the Plaintiff's questioning filed by the Defendants goes in “as is” and becomes evidence at large. 2. Read-in Not Binding on Court It has long been the law of Alberta that when a party reads in extracts from an examination for discovery of an opponent, that becomes evidence which he adopts but he must take both the benefit and the burden, if any, of that evidence… However, where, as here, the parties also give evidence at trial, the trial judge is free, as he was here, to exercise his normal function of assessing credibility, finding facts, and reaching conclusions from all the evidence, and is not bound to accept those discovery extracts read in …Mackow v. Sood (1993), 141 A.R. 233 (C.A.), at 236-37, per curiam. In Johannessen v. First Canadian Insurance Corp. (1996), 194 A.R. 97 (Q.B.), Wilson J., at pp. 103-104 made the following comments about reading-in from discovery: In many areas of proof in this case, counsel for the plaintiff made much of discovery put in by the defendant as part of his case. He referred to the well known case of Hayhurst v. Innisfail Motors Ltd., [1935] 1 W.W.R. 385 (Alberta Supreme Court Appellate Div.), for the proposition that as the defendant had read answers in, he must be taken to have adopted those parts of those answers which were against his case. The defendant did indeed read in a great deal of material. In many instances, one wonders why he did so. For example, he read in from the plaintiff's discovery the plaintiff's forceful assertion that at the time of the policy application, he, the plaintiff, was in good health. One must wonder if he is stuck with this answer. During the course of argument I brought to the attention of counsel the notations on this matter which appear in Civil Procedure Guide, Stevenson and Côté, p. 645 of the 1992 Edition, where the question is posed: “Do the passages read in from the opponent's answers on discovery bind the party reading them in so that he cannot contradict them?” The learned authors say: “Many cases comment on the futility of reading in answers contrary to one's case[”], citing as an example Collins v. Belgian Dry Cleaners Dyers & Furriers Ltd. (1951), 4 W.W.R. (N.S.) 241 (Sask. C.A.). The cases, including Hayhurst v. Innisfail Motors are referred to, including many that say, no, there is no binding effect, and others to the effect that there is no general rule, and others to the effect that such evidence may prevail, particularly if there is no other evidence to refute it, and the opponent does not testify. In this case the opponent did testify, and there is other evidence to the contrary to some of the answers the plaintiff now relies upon. In my opinion this leaves it to the trial judge to weigh all the available evidence, and it is open to him to discard the answers read in if he finds other credible evidence which is reliable and to the contrary. The evidence read in did complicate the case. I suggest that all lawyers would be well advised to put at the top of their briefs, the comment of the authors of the Civil Procedure Guide: “But whether or not bad answers bind one, why read them in the first place.” In Verwoerd v. Verwoerd, 2017 ABQB 272, Justice Renke discussed the use of read-in evidence: [25]… Read-in evidence is evidence to be considered with all the other evidence in the case as determined by the trier of fact in light of the burden of proof. Justice Topolniski stated the following at paras 10–13 of 581257 Alberta Ltd v Aujla[2011 ABQB 39]: [10] The use and effect of evidence read in from examinations for discovery has been canvassed in a number of Alberta authorities. The law concerning the effect of evidence read in from an opposing party's examination for discovery is concisely stated in Stevenson & Côté, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2002 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2002) at p. 171: The utmost caution is needed in selecting questions to read in at trial. They do not fully bind the party reading them in; he or she can lead evidence which contradicts them. But when read in, they become evidence for and against all parties (according to their content), so they might even lose the suit for the party reading them in. [11] As stated in Hayhurst v. Innisfail Motors Ltd., 1935 CanLII 237 (AB CA), [1935] 1 W.W.R. 385 at 389 (Alta. S.C.A.D.): Under the Rule a party need not put in more of the examination than he wishes and subject to the right of the Judge to have read any other part so connected with what is put in as being necessary to make its meaning clear he need not be affected by any part of the examination other than serves his purpose, but when he puts in evidence any portion of such examination it becomes evidence and it requires no rule to make it tell against him if it has that effect. He must take the burden, if any there be, with the benefit he receives. [12] Examination for discovery evidence adopted by a party at trial is like any other evidence. It may be contradicted or qualified by other evidence led by either of the parties and the court may assess its value in the context of all of the evidence presented on the issue. It does not become conclusive evidence when it is read in and the court is not bound to accept and follow it any more than it would in terms of other evidence (Michel v. Lafrentz, 1999 ABCA 21 (CanLII), 232 A.R. 62 at para. 14, leave to appeal to the S.C.C. denied (2000), 255 A.R. 400 (note)). In Mackow v. Sood, (1993), 1993 ABCA 152 (CanLII), 141 A.R. 233 at para. 15 (C.A.), the court explained that: … when a party reads in extracts from an examination for discovery of an opponent, that becomes evidence which he adopts but he must take both the benefit and the burden, if any, of that evidence … However, where, as here, the parties also give evidence at trial, the trial judge is free, as he was here, to exercise his normal function of assessing credibility, finding facts, and reaching conclusions from all the evidence, and is not bound to accept those discovery extracts read in (Ure v. Fagnan (1957), 1957 CanLII 440 (AB CA), 22 W.W.R. (N.S.) 289 (Alta. C.A.) at 308-309; affirmed 1958 CanLII 47 (SCC), [1958] S.C.R. 377). [13] The evidence in the present case is such that it is open to me to reject the answers read in by the Plaintiff where there is other more reliable evidence to the contrary. For the reasons discussed, I have done so concerning the examination for discovery evidence about admitted dates of conversions, which I do not find to determinative. [26] Furthermore, the reading-in party is not confined to any particular set of inferences supported by passages read-in. Read-in evidence could support both unfavourable and favourable inferences from the reading-in party's perspective. The reading-in party would have the job of showing that the inferences supportive of its position are the inferences that should be drawn by the trier of fact. 3. Use of Other Parties' Examination In Edmonton (City) v. Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc. et al., 2000 ABQB 882, 2000 CarswellAlta 1394, 279 A.R. 1, 88 Alta. L.R. (3d) 283, Lee J. had before him the issue of whether in argument the plaintiff City could rely on examination for discovery answers read-in by the defendant from the discovery of the third party. “The City justified this on the basis that the evidence had been read in against Rotek [third party] and it should not matter which party did the reading in” (p. 12). The parties had agreed that the City could read-in from the discovery of Rotek, regardless of who conducted it. Lee J. held that, even if portions of Rotek's discovery had been read-in by another party (i.e., Lovat), the City could not rely on those read-ins from Rotek's discovery unless the City had itself read them in. At pp. 14-15, his Lordship said: The admissions are those of Rotek. As a result, there is no concern that use of the evidence would be unfair to Rotek. However, I question whether the City should be entitled to take the benefit of the evidence read in by Lovat as it does not suffer the potential burden of those read-ins. … In the present case, the City chose to read in various passages from the examination for discovery of Rotek's officer and an employee. Certain of these were the same passages read in by Lovat. …. Given the agreement between counsel as to which parties which (sic) could make use of the discovery evidence, the City was entitled to read in any passage which it might choose from the transcript of the examinations of Rotek's officer and employee. I assume that there were reasons for the choices made by counsel in terms of the read-ins selected. If the City chose not to read in a passage, it cannot now attempt to rely on that evidence. In summary, I hold that Rotek is not entitled to make use of the discovery evidence of Lovat as against the City nor is the City entitled to make use of Lovat's read-ins against Rotek. It might be possible for counsel to avoid this problem if they agreed that a party could both read-in from a discovery conducted by another, and rely on portions of examinations for discovery read-in at trial by another party. In San Francisco Gifts Ltd., Re, 2004 ABQB 229, 2004 CarswellAlta 362, 360 A.R. 394, Topolniski J. said such an agreement must be on the record. At p 396, her Ladyship said: In an examination for discovery an agreement between two parties adverse in interest to use a transcript as though made by both must be on the record (Soroka v. Skjoth et al. (1997), 207 A.R. 1 (Q.B. Master)). See also Stevenson and Côté, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2003 (Edmonton, Juriliber, 2003) at p. 181. This form of agreement is necessary because otherwise, under rule 214, use of the transcript is limited. In CCS Corp. v. Secure Energy Services Inc., 2013 ABQB 662, 2013 CarswellAlta 2407, a defendant (Pembina Pipeline Corporation) brought an application for summary judgment. In response to the application, the Plaintiff filed an affidavit (of a Mr. Evans). In allowing an application to strike out certain parts of that affidavit, Chief Justice Wittmann held that Mr. Evans could not simply rely on evidence given by other parties during Questioning. His Lordship said, at paragraph 11: 11 In my view, to the extent that Mr. Evans' beliefs, as set out in the Evans Affidavit, are based upon a review of answers given by co-defendants in this action in the course of questioning, those beliefs are not admissible in evidence on this application. To admit them would be to violate ARC 5.31. To put the matter another way, one cannot “back door” such evidence by reviewing the transcript of Questioning and then summarizing it in the form of an affidavit. 4. Cross-Examination Using a Transcript by another party in the same action In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Wood Group Mustang (Canada) Inc., 2017 ABQB 106, 2017 CarswellAlta 298, a Mr. Wilkinson was a past employee of the plaintiff. At pre-trial questioning, he was produced by the plaintiff and cross-examined by the defendant. However, at trial it was the defendant which called Mr. Wilkinson to give evidence, and he was cross-examined by the plaintiff. “In cross-examination at trial, [the plaintiff] wished to put to him some evidence from the transcript of that questioning by [the defendant], to challenge the recollection of Mr. Wilkinson and thus his credibility” (paragraph 459). The defendant submitted that Rule 5.31 “essentially forbids this as that section deals with the use that may be made of the transcript of any questioning or answers to written questions” (paragraph 461). Justice Nation permitted the plaintiff to so use the questioning transcript. Her Ladyship said: 466 The reason behind rule 5.31 is to speak to the use of a transcript as evidence before the Court. The restrictions are set so counsel may question on an affidavit, or conduct pre-trial questioning, with the knowledge that the evidence adduced can only be used by them, against the party questioned. 467 The rule deals with who may use the evidence; it does not address the use of the transcript to impeach a witness. Rule 5.31 is permissive: it says how the Court may direct a party in using a transcript as evidence at trial. It does not say that it is the only use that can ever be made of a questioning transcript. 468 The attempt here is not for the Plaintiff to use the transcript as evidence as part of their case or to have the witness adopt evidence, rather it is to impeach his credibility by showing that he has testified differently on a previous occasion about a subject on which he testified under oath at trial. 469 The most analogous situation is where transcripts from the questioning or examination for discovery in one action are used in another action for exactly this purpose. This impeachment by using previously sworn evidence is allowed in another action only if the confidentiality associated with that transcript is waived. This often occurs if a judge finds the truth-seeking use of the transcript justifies relieving counsel of any confidentiality that may be associated with the transcript. 470 As a result I allowed the Plaintiff to put to Mr. Wilkinson in cross-examination, portions of his transcript from the questioning of any of the other parties (that will include the Defendant here or other previous Defendants), if the purpose was to put to him a previous inconsistent statement solely for the reason of impeachment. 5. Practice Regarding Read-ins—Contradicting the Witness With these exceptions, it is my view that it is the better practice, and one that should be adopted in Alberta (if it has not already been so adopted), that the respondent (usually the defendant) to any such burden of proof should put potential admissions, as well as inconsistent statements, to the applicant (usually the plaintiff) party or officer that testifies prior to the respondent's case, while that witness is on the stand. I will restate this more explicitly. With respect to the question of credibility, if the respondent counsel perceives that an answer given on the stand is in contradiction with an answer in the transcript of the examination-for-discovery, then the witness should be confronted in cross-examination with a reading from the transcript taking place and the witness being challenged. With respect to admissions, it is a very simple matter for counsel to summarize the admissions in the transcript that he or she wishes to establish in evidence and to have the party (or officer of a corporate party) confirm those admissions in cross-examination. The witness can either confirm or deny the admissions. If they are confirmed, a read-in is not necessary. If the admissions are denied then I am of the view that it is the proper time to put any alleged admissions from the transcript to the witness and have the matter resolved, and if denial is still prevailing, to later read-in the admissions. This practice is important for a number of reasons, not the least of which is to deal with the matter while it is fresh at hand, and, more important, to prevent undue rebuttal, especially when rebuttal might take place some days later (particularly in the case of long trial), or when such a witness may need to be recalled from a distance. Guarantee Co. of North America v. Beasse (1992), 124 A.R. 161 (Q.B.), at 227-28, per Rooke J. In Edmonton (City) v. Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc., 2000 ABQB 226, 2000 CarswellAlta 332, 262 A.R. 236, 82 Alta. L.R. (3d) 187, Mr. Justice Lee commented on Rooke J.'s decision in Guarantee Co. of North America v. Beasse (1991), 150 A.R. 241 (Q.B.). Lee J., at p. 194, agreed with Rooke J.'s comment that “with respect to challenging the credibility of a witness, the most appropriate procedure is that the witness be challenged on any alleged previous inconsistent statement in cross-examination, when an alleged contradictory statement is referred to in examination-in-chief (as in a hostile witness situation) or in cross-examination.” However, Lee J. did not agree that the “preferred practice” referred to by Rooke J. has been adopted in Alberta. Lee J. concluded that a failure to follow the “preferred practice” would not result in an exclusion of the evidence. At p. 195, he said: Whether or not there is a preferred procedure, in my view the defendant cannot be precluded from reading-in admissions given the plain wording of Rule 214(1). … I do not believe that a defendant's right to read-in admissions of the plaintiff can be denied as a result of the defendant's failure to follow this procedure. Mr. Justice Lee then made the following order (at p. 196): In view of my assessment of the law on this issue, I find that Rotek [Third Pary] is entitled to read-in admissions made by the officers of the City [Plaintiff] and Lovat [Defendant] to the extent that those admissions do not contradict the evidence given by those witnesses at trial. The same would apply to admissions of employees if the officer on examination for discovery acknowledged that the evidence of the employees is information of the the City/Lovat. The City and Lovat may recall those witnesses in rebuttal and ask the witnesses to explain the admissions which have been read-in from discovery. With respect, this ruling is troublesome. Having said that “the defendant cannot be precluded from reading-in admissions”, his Lordship then precludes reading-in discovery admissions of witnesses which contradict that witnesses's trial evidence. Further, Lee, J. then says that the witnesses whose discovery admissions have been read-in may be recalled in rebuttal. However, if no contradictory examination for discovery admissions have been allowed to be read-in, what justifies the calling of rebuttal evidence? Indeed, even if a contradictory examination for discovery admission is allowed to be read-in, what justifies rebuttal evidence? A new issue has not been raised (i.e., the issue has already been addressed in the witness's evidence at trial or there would be no conradiction), and the content of the witness's statement at examination for discovery comes as no surprise to anyone at the trial. 6. When Is a Read-in Considered Complete? … the proper test for the assessment of the completeness of a proposed read-in was fairness to the party based on the specific question asked rather than on the topic addressed in the questions. In other words, the objective was not to require the opposing party to read-in everything the examined party said on a topic, but to ensure that the whole answer the party examined gave to a question was read-in…155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (1993), 147 A.R. 90 (Q.B.), at 92, per Veit J. In Peppler Estate v. Lee, 2019 ABQB 144, 2019 CarswellAlta 365, Madam Justice Topolniski said: [167] The purpose of [Rule 5.31(3)] is to ensure that the Court is not misled by reading isolated parts of the transcript. In considering the question, the Court examines the read-in with a view to ensuring fairness. [168] The law interpreting the predecessor of r 5.31, former R 214(4), remains good law.[35] In Edmonton (City) v Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc,[36] the Court explains that the Rule's purpose is: [To] allow the witness to add to half an answer or to clarify a passage which has been taken out of context or is otherwise misleading. The test for letting the party or parties opposite supplement or augment the read-in in any particular instance is “connectedness” with the part being read-in. [169]“Connectedness” does not always require “adjacency.” W. Stevenson and J. Côté's Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, Vol 3 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2003), at 45-10 notes that the rule allows additional answers, but they must be explanatory and connected. It is the specific question, not the topic that is to be considered: The test for using the rule allowing the opposite party to add additional answers to a read in is whether the additional answers are both explanatory and connected. One cannot insist on having go in, all that one ever said on a topic. The question is fairness based on the questions asked, not the mere content of the answer. The test is the specific question, not the topic. The idea is to get the full answer, but not the last word on a topic. … Among the tests for “connection” are continuity of thought or subject matter, the reason the evidence was introduced in the first place, and fairness so that the entire answer of a witness and not just part of his answer is before the court on a particular subject. [Footnotes omitted.] [170] In Murphy Oil Co v Predator Corp,[37] the Court noted: The authorities are clear that R. 214(4) cannot be used to put before the Court all that the witness has said on a particular topic. It is limited to adding the rest of a specific answer or clarifying a passage which has been taken out of context or may be misleading (Edmonton (City) v. Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc. et al. (2000), 262 A.R. 244 (Q.B.) at para.19, citing 155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (1993), 21 C.P.C. (3d) 159 (Alta.Q.B.) at 163; and Dix v. Canada, 2002 ABQB 196 (CanLII); [2002] A.J. No. 238 (Q.B.) at para.2). The issue here is whether the Predator Defendants' proposed additional read-ins are so connected to the question or topic referred to by Apache in its read-ins that the proposed read-ins should be allowed. 7. Lawyer's Answer Binding Client? When does a lawyer's answer at discovery bind a client being examined? I accept that a lawyer's word usually binds the client. However, the circumstances of each case must be examined. I agree with the applicants that the counsel of perfection on discovery is for the questioner to ask the party being examined if they adopt their lawyer's answer. However … mere adherence to this practice cannot decide whether the lawyer's answer binds the client. The words used by a lawyer in answering discovery questions for a client might establish that the client formally adopts the lawyer's answer, even though the word “adopt” is never used. For example, if a lawyer intervened after a question had been asked and, perhaps after having off the record discussions with the client, said: “I have been instructed to reply …”, the party opposite and the court would be entitled to take the lawyer's words as those of the client. The fact that there has been no objection by the client to his lawyer answering questions for him cannot decide the issue raised on this motion. A party has a lawyer representing him at discovery precisely to deal with the legal issues; a client should not be expected to have to deal with his own lawyer's conduct during discovery. Discovery is a dynamic, interactive, process; it is quite different in style to those processes which are taken by a party in privacy such as formulation of pleadings, or answers to written interrogatories, or solicitors' undertakings, or formal admissions of facts under the Criminal Code. In all the latter processes, it is reasonable to assume that a lawyer acts on the authority of his client, and the words of the lawyer will bind the client. However, in discovery one question follows another; there is no reason to suppose in this particular case, for example, that Mr. Vaage [the lawyer] and Mr. Azrieli [his client] had time for consultation before Mr. Vaage said the words quoted at lines 7 to 12 of p. 125. In these circumstances, it is not fair to impose Mr. Vaage's words on Mr. Azrieli, without more. As the answer to undertaking this very example demonstrates, important questions of solicitor-client privilege could be breached by the solicitor when the give and take of the questioning process has not afforded the client the opportunity of determining whether he wants to waive his privilege in order to have his solicitor answer questions. 155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (1993), 147 A.R. 90 (Q.B.), at 95-96, per Veit J. 8. Effect of Mary Carter Agreements In Syncrude Canada v. Canadian Bechtel Ltd. (1994), 16 Alta. L.R. (3d) 153 (C.A.), the Alberta Court of Appeal commented on the effect of a Mary Carter agreement on the ability to read-in discovery answers of a defendant against the plaintiff (see discussion of “Mary Carter agreement”, infra). In Syncrude Canada v. Canadian Bechtel Ltd., the Court of Appeal said the following, at pp. 154-55: The respondents sued the defendants alleging faulty or inadequate equipment supplied and installed in the plaintiffs' plant. The defendants third-partied the appellant, and the appellant examined the defendants for discovery. After the discovery of one defendant, and part way through the discovery of another, the plaintiff made Mary Carter agreements with the defendants. Under these agreements, the defendants are to pay (or have paid) set amounts to the respondents, and will have no further liability to the respondents. But the defendants will stay in the suit, and the respondents and the defendants will cooperate in opposing the appellant… The court ruled as follows, at pp. 155-58: Ordinarily discovery answers can be put into evidence at trial only against the party who gave the answers (or whose designated officer gave the answers). That is common ground. However, counsel for the appellant points out R. 214(3), and says that it is not confined to employees of the party. That counsel argues that R. 214(3) is not confined to persons whose attendance at trial cannot be obtained. He suggests that it would be ‘just and convenient’ to do what he seeks, using that subrule. The justice arises, he argues, because the Mary Carter agreements create virtual identity of interest and full cooperation between the defendants whose officer answered, and the respondents against whom he wishes to use the answers. He suggests that a Mary Carter agreement creates a very unusual situation, and that what he wishes would not be a very wide interpretation of R. 214(3)… We do not see that identity of interest or close cooperation, or an agreement to cooperate closely, produce conditions which make it just to visit the out-of-court evidence or admissions of one party on the other. Even the discovery answers of employees are not, without more, admissions by their employers. (There are cases discussing when they may be shown to be information which the employer had, but the scope of that is not really germane to the present case, for no such limited use is suggested here.) When two parties at the time of discovery have very similar interests and are cooperating and are bound to cooperate, that greatly reduces or excludes the risk that one party might give discovery answers designed to help himself but designed to hurt the other party, or which have that effect because the two parties' interests diverge. But that is true of only part of one of the two sets of discovery answers here in question, and true of none of the discovery answers by the other defendant. The Mary Carter agreements were made after one discovery, and during the other. Therefore, about three-quarters of the answers were given when the person answering and the defendant nominating him were at arm's length with the respondent and the respondents were then suing the parties being examined, for very large sums. Nor is that the only risk in using A's answers against B. There is also the risk that the party answering may investigate carelessly, or speak carelessly when answering questions. The answer may be wrong. It is just that a party's own careless answer be admissible against him; he has no one to blame for his carelessness but himself. And much the same thing is true of a designated corporate officer, for a corporation otherwise has no mouth to speak. In Alberta, the corporation chooses its own officer under R. 214. But one cannot say that of the present case. It is highly unlikely that the respondents had any say whatever in the choice of the two corporate officers whose answers are now in issue, nor in the investigation conducted to inform them so that they might answer, nor in the general briefing about how to conduct themselves during the examination for discovery. Nor do such careful investigation and briefing guarantee accurate answers, as every Canadian barrister knows. In sum therefore, it is unfair to put into evidence against a person an admission by a different person, whether or not the two now have similar interests, friendship, and cooperation… Maybe R. 214(3) could be read in a broad and loose sense as the appellant suggests. We tend to doubt it, but need not decide that. Even if it could be so read, it would be unjust to extend it to a situation like the present. And nothing in the Rules allows the appellant to read in these answers against other parties. In Pettey v. Avis Car Inc. (1993), 103 D.L.R. (4th) 298 (Ont. Gen. Div.), the court discussed “Mary Carter agreements”. At pp. 304-305, Ferrier J. said: The expression “Mary Carter agreement” has its origin in the Florida case Booth v. Mary Carter Paint Co. 202 So. 2d 8 (Fla. App., 1967). Cases in the United States have indicated that a typical Mary Carter agreement contains the following features: 1. The contracting defendant guarantees the plaintiff a certain monetary recovery and the exposure of that defendant is “capped” at that amount. 2. The contracting defendant remains in the lawsuit. 3. The contracting defendant's liability is decreased in direct proportion to the increase in the non-contracting defendant's liability. 4. The agreement is kept secret. . . . . . In reported decisions, the majority of the courts in the United States which have considered the validity of Mary Carter agreements have allowed them to stand provided the agreement is disclosed to the parties and to the court… At p. 308, the learned trial judge said: Apparently, Mary Carter agreements have become commonplace in the majority of states in the United States and are increasingly in use in Canada … there is apparently no Canadian decision that has found them to be invalid. At pp. 310-11, Ferrier J. discussed the conditions that must be met: The agreement must be disclosed to the parties and to the court as soon as the agreement is made. The non-contracting defendants must be advised immediately because the agreement may well have an impact on the strategy and line of cross-examination to be pursued and evidence to be led by them. The non-contracting parties must also be aware of the agreement so that they can properly assess the steps being taken from that point forward by the plaintiff and the contracting defendants. In short, procedural fairness requires immediate disclosure. Most importantly, the court must be informed immediately so that it can properly fulfil its role in controlling its process in the interests of fairness and justice to all parties. . . . . . Excepting the dollar amounts, it is rather obvious that all of the terms of the agreement must be disclosed, especially for the purpose of enabling the court to control its own process… The disclosure of the dollar amounts is patently in the discretion of the court. 9. Admission at Trial of Evidence Not Objected to at Discovery … I am firmly of the opinion that a trial judge has power to exclude inadmissible or irrelevant discovery evidence tendered by an opponent as part of his case even though not objected to on examination. Saskatchewan Mutual Insurance Co. v. Lyle (1959), 28 W.W.R. 155 (B.C. C.A.), at 166, per Davey J.A. In Wright v. Schultz (1992), 135 A.R. 58, the Court of Appeal said, at pp. 60-62: Should rulings on the admissibility at trial of answers given or sought on discovery be made during the discovery or at trial? It was suggested at the hearing of this appeal that if at trial a party chose to read in any part of an examination of the opposite party, the trial judge could not exclude it. This argument was based on the wording of rule 214(1)… If this argument were correct, questions of admissibility would have to be determined during examinations for discovery, rather than at trial. However, in my view it is not correct. If a trial judge decides for any reason that the part of an examination which a party wishes to read is inadmissible, he must exclude it. I do not think that rule 214(1) can or should be read as saying anything to the contrary. Further, in my view questions of admissibility are best dealt with in the context of the trial, not during discovery. Support for this proposition can be found in Cominco Ltd. v. Phillips Cables Ltd. et al., [1987] 3 W.W.R. 562, (Sask. C.A.). In Cominco Mr. Justice Cameron, writing for the court, referred (at p. 567) to the approach taken by Mr. Justice McLelland in Ratner Realty Ltd. v. Saskatchewan Telecommunications, [1981] Sask. D. 3628-01 (Q.B.). In that case Mr. Justice McLelland was asked to decide whether certain questions could be asked on an examination for discovery. In particular he was asked to decide whether the responses to those questions would be admissible at trial. He refused to do so and expressed his reasons as follows: It is possible that after having heard the answers to the questions put to the witnesses, counsel for the plaintiff will not attempt to introduce the evidence at trial. If he does, the trial judge will be in a better position to judge the admissibility of the evidence in question, and, if admissible, under what conditions it should be admitted or the weight to be attached to it. Mr. Justice Cameron summarized this approach, which the court approved, at p. 568: He thus limited himself to broad relevance, leaving issues of admissibility and weight to be determined at trial. It is true that the Saskatchewan rule relating to the use of examinations for discovery was not then identical to rule 214(1). Rule 239 of the Saskatchewan Rules of Practice and Procedure then read: 239. Any party at the trial of an action or issue … may subject to all just exceptions, use in evidence any part of the examination of the opposite party … (emphasis added) However, I do not think that the fact that the phrase underlined above is not in rule 204(1) means that the practice in Alberta is or should be different from that outlined in the Cominco judgment. It seems clear that the relevance of evidence is to be determined at trial. In Czuy et al. v. Mitchell and Edmonton General Hospital (1976), 1 Alta. L.R. (2d) 97 (C.A.), Mr. Justice Prowse, writing for the majority, suggested this at p. 100. Referring to an application for an order directing a party to reattend to be examined for discovery and to answer certain questions, he said: In my view, a court, in ruling on such applications, should not unduly restrict an examination by excluding questions broadly related to the issues when it appears that their relevance may well be resolved by other evidence not before the court on the application. A clear statement of this proposition can be found in Drake v. Overland and Southam Press Ltd. (1979), 19 A.R. 472 (C.A.), where Mr. Justice Laycraft (as he then was), writing for the court, said in relation to examinations for discovery (at p. 484): Only those questions which are clearly irrelevant should be rejected at this stage since in the absence of all the evidence to be produced at trial the Court can form only a general impression as to their relevance. It is therefore the responsibility of the trial judge to determine relevance in light of the evidence at the trial. It follows that a trial judge is obliged to exclude from evidence any part of an examination that a party wishes to read which he finds to be irrelevant. Similarly, in my view, it is the responsibility of the trial judge to decide whether evidence is inadmissible for reasons not related to relevancy. He must exclude from evidence any part of an examination that a party wishes to read which he finds to be inadmissible. The Court of Appeal went on to discuss how one can properly make objections while discovery is being read in at trial. At p. 62 it said: Counsel for the appellant expressed concern that if counsel for the respondent read in parts of the examination of the appellant, he would not be able to object to inadmissible questions and answers quickly enough to prevent the jury from hearing them. If counsel has serious concerns in this regard during the trial, he can discuss them with the trial judge in the absence of the jury, and before any parts of the examination are read. He can ask that the trial judge take whatever steps would be most effective to avoid such a problem. For example, the trial judge could ask that counsel for the respondent give him the questions and answers he intends to read in advance. Or he could order that counsel for the respondent give these questions and answers to opposing counsel in advance so that he would have a chance to object in a timely fashion. 10. Hearsay (i) Effect of hearsay Counsel for the appellant argued that he should not be required to answer such questions for the following reasons. He said that any answers which the appellant might give as to what others had told him would be hearsay and inadmissible to prove the truth of what he had been told. Counsel argued, therefore, that the answers could not be used under rule 214(1) … I do not agree with counsel for the appellant that any answers which he might give as to what others had told him would be inadmissible to prove the truth of what he had been told. They would be admissible for this purpose if the appellant adopted them or indicated a belief in the truth of their contents (R. v. Streu (1989), A.R. 356 (S.C.C.)). Beyond that, the answers might be admissible for other purposes. If admissible, the answers could be used under rule 214(1) … There is clear authority in British Columbia (Haswell v. Burns & Jackson Logging Co., [1947] 2 W.W.R. 394 (B.C. C.A.); Freeman v. Allied Collection Agencies Canada Ltd. (1965), 51 W.W.R. (N.S.) 254 (B.C. S.C.)), and in Manitoba (Dowhoszyja v. Kachor, [1982] 3 W.W.R. 569 (C.A.)), for the proposition that during an examination for discovery the party being examined must answer questions about what other people have told him. In Alberta there is equally clear authority for this proposition at the trial level (Cobble v. Mills and Swarich, [1947] 2 W.W.R. 790 at 796 to 799 (Alta. T.D.); Tiedemann v. Basiuk et al. (1977), 4 Alta. L.R. (2d) 12 at 14 (Q.B.)). Wright v. Schultz (1992), 135 A.R. 58 at 60, 62 (C.A.). (ii) Usefulness of hearsay Finally, while one purpose of an examination for discovery is to obtain admissions which can be used at trial, it is not the only purpose. An examination for discovery also has as its goal to enable the party examining to better assess his own case and that of the opposite party. A hearsay answer, even if it is not admissible at trial, may assist in this regard. Wright v. Schultz, supra, at 62. 11. Court Practice on R. 5.31(3) Applications When a rule 214(4) issue is raised, the court examines the read-in on a question by question basis with a view to ensuring, in fairness to the party being examined, that the party's complete answer is read in. Here, in some situations, a longer read-in is required. 155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (1993), 147 A.R. 90 (Q.B.), at 92, per Veit J. In Edmonton (City) v. Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc., 2000 ABQB 143, 2000 CarswellAlta 213, 260 A.R. 245, Lee J. said, at p. 254: Rule 214(4) relates to read ins. Its purpose is to allow the witness to add to half an answer, or to clarify a passage which has been taken out of context or otherwise is misleading. The same principle can and should be applied to a situation such as the present one where a part of the examination for discovery has been put to a party in cross-examination. 12. Meaning of “if it is so connected” in old R. 214(4) (current R. 5.31) … R. 214(4) permits the extra read-in “… if it is so connected with the part so used that the first mentioned part ought not be used without the other part.” It is, therefore, incumbent upon the [party invoking the rule] to demonstrate this connection and for me to ask what is meant by “if it is so connected” and “ought” not to be used… Our own Court of Appeal in Rogers v. Weir, [1927] 3 W.W.R. 177, [23 Alta. L.R. 28], considered the meaning of the words “connected with” and “ought not to be used.” Mr. Justice of Appeal Beck defined one in terms of the other; and said [p. 178]: The present Rule entitles the party, part of whose examination is being used by the opposite party, to have any further part put which ‘ought’ to be put in, that is to say, as said by Cotton, L.J., in Lyell v. Kennedy (1884), 27 Ch. D. 1 at p. 15 …‘which is fairly connected with’ the part proffered—‘connected in sense or substance.’Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. (1993), 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 337 (Q.B.), at 341-42, per MacCallum J. In Edmonton (City) v. Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc., 2000 ABQB 265, 2000 CarswellAlta 393, 265 A.R. 285, Lee J., at p. 287, said: The test for letting the party or parties opposite supplement or augment the read-in in any particular instance is “connectedness” with the part being read-in. In my previous Reasons in this action in regard to the scope of cross and reexamination [(2000), 260 A.R. 245 (Q.B.)], I indicated that “connectedness” does not always require “adjacency”. His Lordship was referring to the fact that in his previous Reasons he had permitted opposing counsel to make reference to a portion of the transcript which was more than 100 pages away from the segment being used by examining counsel. As long as the portions were “connected”, they need not be “adjacent” to each other in the transcript. In 155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (1993), 147 A.R. 90 (Q.B.), Veit J. said, at p. 92: …[T]he proper test for the assessment of the completeness of a proposed read-in was fairness to the party based on the specific question asked rather than on the topic addressed in the questions. In other words, the objective was not to require the opposing party to read-in everything the examined party said on a topic, but to ensure that the whole answer the party examined gave to a question was read-in. 13. Use of Employee and Representative Transcripts Together In Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. (1993), 20 Alta. L.R. (3d) 337 (Q.B.), MacCallum J. was presiding at a trial in which the plaintiff was reading in from discovery certain questions and answers given by a Mr. Sambell, an employee of the defendant. The defendant applied, pursuant to R. 214(4), for the court to use part of the discovery transcript of the defendant's representative, a Mr. Phannenstiel. In the words of MacCallum J., the read-ins from Mr. Sambell were “not being read in directly, but rather through the defendant's representative Phannenstiel as information of the defendant”. For an explanation of that process, see “Use of Examinations of Employees”, infra. After the read-ins by the Plaintiff, “the defendants rose to apply to use not another part of the same examination of Sambell, but rather Phannenstiel's responses to the … generic question in which he said in effect that he indeed had information which was contrary or inconsistent with Sambell's evidence”. Should the defendants be permitted to use that evidence pursuant to R. 214(4)? At pp. 340-41, his Lordship said: Nobody argues, I suppose, that a party could demand that B's discovery answers be read in to clarify something in A's discovery answers; but we are not here dealing with A and B. We are dealing with only A, Stearns Catalytic. I am simply not listening to the answers of Sambell being read in as his answers. Notionally, I am listening to the information of the defendant Stearns Catalytic. Were it otherwise, Sambell's answers as I pointed out above could not be read in. So here is what the plaintiffs propose. Although the defendant's officer has responded affirmatively to the … generic question and has provided the particulars required, the plaintiffs may use these responses for informational purposes; but the defendants are precluded from using particulars of the responses by way of explanation or clarification under R. 214(4). To me, this is unfair. To again emphasize the notional aspect of this situation, the person whose evidence was read in by the plaintiffs is Stearns Catalytic. This point was made repeatedly by the plaintiffs in support of their argument made earlier in this trial that read-ins such as they have made on October the 19th are not hearsay and are within the purview of the rules which do not authorize the use at trial of discovery answers of employees, per se. That covers I think the objection that the examination of a different person is being used to clarify the read-in. MacCallum J. then discussed other aspects of the application. He concluded by saying, at p. 342: The plaintiffs have expressed concern that they might be bound by the additional read-ins as part of their case. They need not be. Anything extra which might be read in at the defendant's request simply becomes evidence in the case generally to be judged by the ordinary Rules of Evidence and to be accorded the weight which it merits.

I will restate this more explicitly.

With respect to the question of credibility, if the respondent counsel perceives that an answer given on the stand is in contradiction with an answer in the transcript of the examination-for-discovery, then the witness should be confronted in cross-examination with a reading from the transcript taking place and the witness being challenged.

With respect to admissions, it is a very simple matter for counsel to summarize the admissions in the transcript that he or she wishes to establish in evidence and to have the party (or officer of a corporate party) confirm those admissions in cross-examination.
The witness can either confirm or deny the admissions.
If they are confirmed, a read-in is not necessary.

If the admissions are denied then I am of the view that it is the proper time to put any alleged admissions from the transcript to the witness and have the matter resolved, and if denial is still prevailing, to later read-in the admissions.

This practice is important for a number of reasons, not the least of which is to deal with the matter while it is fresh at hand, and, more important, to prevent undue rebuttal, especially when rebuttal might take place some days later (particularly in the case of long trial), or when such a witness may need to be recalled from a distance.
