The same would apply to admissions of employees if the officer on examination for discovery acknowledged that the evidence of the employees is information of the the City/Lovat.
The City and Lovat may recall those witnesses in rebuttal and ask the witnesses to explain the admissions which have been read-in from discovery.
With respect, this ruling is troublesome.

Having said that “the defendant cannot be precluded from reading-in admissions”, his Lordship then precludes reading-in discovery admissions of witnesses which contradict that witnesses's trial evidence.
Further, Lee, J. then says that the witnesses whose discovery admissions have been read-in may be recalled in rebuttal.
However, if no contradictory examination for discovery admissions have been allowed to be read-in, what justifies the calling of rebuttal evidence?
Indeed, even if a contradictory examination for discovery admission is allowed to be read-in, what justifies rebuttal evidence?

A new issue has not been raised (i.e., the issue has already been addressed in the witness's evidence at trial or there would be no conradiction), and the content of the witness's statement at examination for discovery comes as no surprise to anyone at the trial.

When Is a Read-in Considered Complete? … the proper test for the assessment of the completeness of a proposed read-in was fairness to the party based on the specific question asked rather than on the topic addressed in the questions.

In other words, the objective was not to require the opposing party to read-in everything the examined party said on a topic, but to ensure that the whole answer the party examined gave to a question was read-in…155569 Canada Ltd. v.
248524 Alberta Ltd.
90 (Q.B.), at 92, per Veit J.
In Peppler Estate v.
Lee, 2019 ABQB 144, 2019 CarswellAlta 365, Madam Justice Topolniski said: [167] The purpose of [Rule 5.31(3)] is to ensure that the Court is not misled by reading isolated parts of the transcript.
In considering the question, the Court examines the read-in with a view to ensuring fairness.

[168] The law interpreting the predecessor of r 5.31, former R 214(4), remains good law.[35] In Edmonton (City) v Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc,[36] the Court explains that the Rule's purpose is: [To] allow the witness to add to half an answer or to clarify a passage which has been taken out of context or is otherwise misleading.
The test for letting the party or parties opposite supplement or augment the read-in in any particular instance is “connectedness” with the part being read-in.
[169]“Connectedness” does not always require “adjacency.” W.
Stevenson and J.
Côté's Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, Vol 3 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2003), at 45-10 notes that the rule allows additional answers, but they must be explanatory and connected.

It is the specific question, not the topic that is to be considered: The test for using the rule allowing the opposite party to add additional answers to a read in is whether the additional answers are both explanatory and connected.
One cannot insist on having go in, all that one ever said on a topic.
The question is fairness based on the questions asked, not the mere content of the answer.
The test is the specific question, not the topic.

The idea is to get the full answer, but not the last word on a topic. … Among the tests for “connection” are continuity of thought or subject matter, the reason the evidence was introduced in the first place, and fairness so that the entire answer of a witness and not just part of his answer is before the court on a particular subject.
[Footnotes omitted.] [170] In Murphy Oil Co v Predator Corp,[37] the Court noted: The authorities are clear that R.
214(4) cannot be used to put before the Court all that the witness has said on a particular topic.
It is limited to adding the rest of a specific answer or clarifying a passage which has been taken out of context or may be misleading (Edmonton (City) v.
Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc. et al.
244 (Q.B.) at para.19, citing 155569 Canada Ltd. v.
248524 Alberta Ltd.
(3d) 159 (Alta.Q.B.) at 163; and Dix v.
Canada, 2002 ABQB 196 (CanLII); [2002] A.J.
No.
238 (Q.B.) at para.2).

The issue here is whether the Predator Defendants' proposed additional read-ins are so connected to the question or topic referred to by Apache in its read-ins that the proposed read-ins should be allowed.
Lawyer's Answer Binding Client?
When does a lawyer's answer at discovery bind a client being examined?
I accept that a lawyer's word usually binds the client.
However, the circumstances of each case must be examined.
I agree with the applicants that the counsel of perfection on discovery is for the questioner to ask the party being examined if they adopt their lawyer's answer.
However … mere adherence to this practice cannot decide whether the lawyer's answer binds the client.
The words used by a lawyer in answering discovery questions for a client might establish that the client formally adopts the lawyer's answer, even though the word “adopt” is never used.

For example, if a lawyer intervened after a question had been asked and, perhaps after having off the record discussions with the client, said: “I have been instructed to reply …”, the party opposite and the court would be entitled to take the lawyer's words as those of the client.
The fact that there has been no objection by the client to his lawyer answering questions for him cannot decide the issue raised on this motion.
A party has a lawyer representing him at discovery precisely to deal with the legal issues; a client should not be expected to have to deal with his own lawyer's conduct during discovery.

Discovery is a dynamic, interactive, process; it is quite different in style to those processes which are taken by a party in privacy such as formulation of pleadings, or answers to written interrogatories, or solicitors' undertakings, or formal admissions of facts under the Criminal Code.
In all the latter processes, it is reasonable to assume that a lawyer acts on the authority of his client, and the words of the lawyer will bind the client.
However, in discovery one question follows another; there is no reason to suppose in this particular case, for example, that Mr.
Vaage [the lawyer] and Mr.
Azrieli [his client] had time for consultation before Mr.
Vaage said the words quoted at lines 7 to 12 of p.
In these circumstances, it is not fair to impose Mr.
Vaage's words on Mr.
Azrieli, without more.

As the answer to undertaking this very example demonstrates, important questions of solicitor-client privilege could be breached by the solicitor when the give and take of the questioning process has not afforded the client the opportunity of determining whether he wants to waive his privilege in order to have his solicitor answer questions.
155569 Canada Ltd. v.
248524 Alberta Ltd.
90 (Q.B.), at 95-96, per Veit J.
Effect of Mary Carter Agreements In Syncrude Canada v.
Canadian Bechtel Ltd.
L.R.

(3d) 153 (C.A.), the Alberta Court of Appeal commented on the effect of a Mary Carter agreement on the ability to read-in discovery answers of a defendant against the plaintiff (see discussion of “Mary Carter agreement”, infra).
In Syncrude Canada v.
Canadian Bechtel Ltd., the Court of Appeal said the following, at pp.
154-55: The respondents sued the defendants alleging faulty or inadequate equipment supplied and installed in the plaintiffs' plant.
The defendants third-partied the appellant, and the appellant examined the defendants for discovery.
After the discovery of one defendant, and part way through the discovery of another, the plaintiff made Mary Carter agreements with the defendants.
Under these agreements, the defendants are to pay (or have paid) set amounts to the respondents, and will have no further liability to the respondents.
But the defendants will stay in the suit, and the respondents and the defendants will cooperate in opposing the appellant… The court ruled as follows, at pp.
155-58: Ordinarily discovery answers can be put into evidence at trial only against the party who gave the answers (or whose designated officer gave the answers).
That is common ground.
However, counsel for the appellant points out R.
214(3), and says that it is not confined to employees of the party.
That counsel argues that R.
214(3) is not confined to persons whose attendance at trial cannot be obtained.
He suggests that it would be ‘just and convenient’ to do what he seeks, using that subrule.

The justice arises, he argues, because the Mary Carter agreements create virtual identity of interest and full cooperation between the defendants whose officer answered, and the respondents against whom he wishes to use the answers.
He suggests that a Mary Carter agreement creates a very unusual situation, and that what he wishes would not be a very wide interpretation of R.

214(3)… We do not see that identity of interest or close cooperation, or an agreement to cooperate closely, produce conditions which make it just to visit the out-of-court evidence or admissions of one party on the other.
Even the discovery answers of employees are not, without more, admissions by their employers.

(There are cases discussing when they may be shown to be information which the employer had, but the scope of that is not really germane to the present case, for no such limited use is suggested here.) When two parties at the time of discovery have very similar interests and are cooperating and are bound to cooperate, that greatly reduces or excludes the risk that one party might give discovery answers designed to help himself but designed to hurt the other party, or which have that effect because the two parties' interests diverge.
But that is true of only part of one of the two sets of discovery answers here in question, and true of none of the discovery answers by the other defendant.
The Mary Carter agreements were made after one discovery, and during the other.

Therefore, about three-quarters of the answers were given when the person answering and the defendant nominating him were at arm's length with the respondent and the respondents were then suing the parties being examined, for very large sums.
Nor is that the only risk in using A's answers against B.
There is also the risk that the party answering may investigate carelessly, or speak carelessly when answering questions.
The answer may be wrong.
It is just that a party's own careless answer be admissible against him; he has no one to blame for his carelessness but himself.
And much the same thing is true of a designated corporate officer, for a corporation otherwise has no mouth to speak.
In Alberta, the corporation chooses its own officer under R.
But one cannot say that of the present case.

It is highly unlikely that the respondents had any say whatever in the choice of the two corporate officers whose answers are now in issue, nor in the investigation conducted to inform them so that they might answer, nor in the general briefing about how to conduct themselves during the examination for discovery.
Nor do such careful investigation and briefing guarantee accurate answers, as every Canadian barrister knows.
In sum therefore, it is unfair to put into evidence against a person an admission by a different person, whether or not the two now have similar interests, friendship, and cooperation… Maybe R.
214(3) could be read in a broad and loose sense as the appellant suggests.
We tend to doubt it, but need not decide that.
Even if it could be so read, it would be unjust to extend it to a situation like the present.
And nothing in the Rules allows the appellant to read in these answers against other parties.
In Pettey v.
Avis Car Inc.
Gen.
Div.), the court discussed “Mary Carter agreements”.
At pp.
304-305, Ferrier J. said: The expression “Mary Carter agreement” has its origin in the Florida case Booth v.
Mary Carter Paint Co.
2d 8 (Fla.
Cases in the United States have indicated that a typical Mary Carter agreement contains the following features: 1.
The contracting defendant guarantees the plaintiff a certain monetary recovery and the exposure of that defendant is “capped” at that amount.
The contracting defendant remains in the lawsuit.
The contracting defendant's liability is decreased in direct proportion to the increase in the non-contracting defendant's liability.
The agreement is kept secret. . . . . .

In reported decisions, the majority of the courts in the United States which have considered the validity of Mary Carter agreements have allowed them to stand provided the agreement is disclosed to the parties and to the court… At p.

308, the learned trial judge said: Apparently, Mary Carter agreements have become commonplace in the majority of states in the United States and are increasingly in use in Canada … there is apparently no Canadian decision that has found them to be invalid.
At pp.
310-11, Ferrier J. discussed the conditions that must be met: The agreement must be disclosed to the parties and to the court as soon as the agreement is made.
The non-contracting defendants must be advised immediately because the agreement may well have an impact on the strategy and line of cross-examination to be pursued and evidence to be led by them.
The non-contracting parties must also be aware of the agreement so that they can properly assess the steps being taken from that point forward by the plaintiff and the contracting defendants.
In short, procedural fairness requires immediate disclosure.
Most importantly, the court must be informed immediately so that it can properly fulfil its role in controlling its process in the interests of fairness and justice to all parties. . . . . .

Excepting the dollar amounts, it is rather obvious that all of the terms of the agreement must be disclosed, especially for the purpose of enabling the court to control its own process… The disclosure of the dollar amounts is patently in the discretion of the court.

Admission at Trial of Evidence Not Objected to at Discovery … I am firmly of the opinion that a trial judge has power to exclude inadmissible or irrelevant discovery evidence tendered by an opponent as part of his case even though not objected to on examination.
Saskatchewan Mutual Insurance Co. v.
C.A.), at 166, per Davey J.A.
In Wright v.
Schultz (1992), 135 A.R.
58, the Court of Appeal said, at pp.
60-62: Should rulings on the admissibility at trial of answers given or sought on discovery be made during the discovery or at trial?
It was suggested at the hearing of this appeal that if at trial a party chose to read in any part of an examination of the opposite party, the trial judge could not exclude it.
This argument was based on the wording of rule 214(1)… If this argument were correct, questions of admissibility would have to be determined during examinations for discovery, rather than at trial.
However, in my view it is not correct.
If a trial judge decides for any reason that the part of an examination which a party wishes to read is inadmissible, he must exclude it.
I do not think that rule 214(1) can or should be read as saying anything to the contrary.
Further, in my view questions of admissibility are best dealt with in the context of the trial, not during discovery.
Support for this proposition can be found in Cominco Ltd. v.
Phillips Cables Ltd. et al., [1987] 3 W.W.R.
562, (Sask.
In Cominco Mr.
Justice Cameron, writing for the court, referred (at p.
567) to the approach taken by Mr.
Justice McLelland in Ratner Realty Ltd. v.
Saskatchewan Telecommunications, [1981] Sask.
D.
In that case Mr.
Justice McLelland was asked to decide whether certain questions could be asked on an examination for discovery.
In particular he was asked to decide whether the responses to those questions would be admissible at trial.

He refused to do so and expressed his reasons as follows: It is possible that after having heard the answers to the questions put to the witnesses, counsel for the plaintiff will not attempt to introduce the evidence at trial.

If he does, the trial judge will be in a better position to judge the admissibility of the evidence in question, and, if admissible, under what conditions it should be admitted or the weight to be attached to it.
Mr.
Justice Cameron summarized this approach, which the court approved, at p.
568: He thus limited himself to broad relevance, leaving issues of admissibility and weight to be determined at trial.
It is true that the Saskatchewan rule relating to the use of examinations for discovery was not then identical to rule 214(1).
Rule 239 of the Saskatchewan Rules of Practice and Procedure then read: 239.

Any party at the trial of an action or issue … may subject to all just exceptions, use in evidence any part of the examination of the opposite party … (emphasis added) However, I do not think that the fact that the phrase underlined above is not in rule 204(1) means that the practice in Alberta is or should be different from that outlined in the Cominco judgment.
It seems clear that the relevance of evidence is to be determined at trial.
In Czuy et al. v.
Mitchell and Edmonton General Hospital (1976), 1 Alta.
L.R.
Justice Prowse, writing for the majority, suggested this at p.

Referring to an application for an order directing a party to reattend to be examined for discovery and to answer certain questions, he said: In my view, a court, in ruling on such applications, should not unduly restrict an examination by excluding questions broadly related to the issues when it appears that their relevance may well be resolved by other evidence not before the court on the application.
A clear statement of this proposition can be found in Drake v.
Overland and Southam Press Ltd.
472 (C.A.), where Mr.
Justice Laycraft (as he then was), writing for the court, said in relation to examinations for discovery (at p.

484): Only those questions which are clearly irrelevant should be rejected at this stage since in the absence of all the evidence to be produced at trial the Court can form only a general impression as to their relevance.
It is therefore the responsibility of the trial judge to determine relevance in light of the evidence at the trial.
It follows that a trial judge is obliged to exclude from evidence any part of an examination that a party wishes to read which he finds to be irrelevant.
Similarly, in my view, it is the responsibility of the trial judge to decide whether evidence is inadmissible for reasons not related to relevancy.
He must exclude from evidence any part of an examination that a party wishes to read which he finds to be inadmissible.
The Court of Appeal went on to discuss how one can properly make objections while discovery is being read in at trial.
At p.

62 it said: Counsel for the appellant expressed concern that if counsel for the respondent read in parts of the examination of the appellant, he would not be able to object to inadmissible questions and answers quickly enough to prevent the jury from hearing them.
If counsel has serious concerns in this regard during the trial, he can discuss them with the trial judge in the absence of the jury, and before any parts of the examination are read.
He can ask that the trial judge take whatever steps would be most effective to avoid such a problem.
For example, the trial judge could ask that counsel for the respondent give him the questions and answers he intends to read in advance.
Or he could order that counsel for the respondent give these questions and answers to opposing counsel in advance so that he would have a chance to object in a timely fashion.
Hearsay (i) Effect of hearsay Counsel for the appellant argued that he should not be required to answer such questions for the following reasons.
He said that any answers which the appellant might give as to what others had told him would be hearsay and inadmissible to prove the truth of what he had been told.

Counsel argued, therefore, that the answers could not be used under rule 214(1) … I do not agree with counsel for the appellant that any answers which he might give as to what others had told him would be inadmissible to prove the truth of what he had been told.
They would be admissible for this purpose if the appellant adopted them or indicated a belief in the truth of their contents (R. v.
Streu (1989), A.R.
Beyond that, the answers might be admissible for other purposes.
If admissible, the answers could be used under rule 214(1) … There is clear authority in British Columbia (Haswell v.
Burns & Jackson Logging Co., [1947] 2 W.W.R.
C.A.); Freeman v.
Allied Collection Agencies Canada Ltd.
S.C.)), and in Manitoba (Dowhoszyja v.
Kachor, [1982] 3 W.W.R.
569 (C.A.)), for the proposition that during an examination for discovery the party being examined must answer questions about what other people have told him.
In Alberta there is equally clear authority for this proposition at the trial level (Cobble v.
Mills and Swarich, [1947] 2 W.W.R.
790 at 796 to 799 (Alta.
T.D.); Tiedemann v.
Basiuk et al.
L.R.
Wright v.
Schultz (1992), 135 A.R.
(ii) Usefulness of hearsay Finally, while one purpose of an examination for discovery is to obtain admissions which can be used at trial, it is not the only purpose.
An examination for discovery also has as its goal to enable the party examining to better assess his own case and that of the opposite party.
A hearsay answer, even if it is not admissible at trial, may assist in this regard.
Wright v.
Schultz, supra, at 62.
Court Practice on R.

5.31(3) Applications When a rule 214(4) issue is raised, the court examines the read-in on a question by question basis with a view to ensuring, in fairness to the party being examined, that the party's complete answer is read in.
Here, in some situations, a longer read-in is required.
155569 Canada Ltd. v.
248524 Alberta Ltd.
90 (Q.B.), at 92, per Veit J.
In Edmonton (City) v.
Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc., 2000 ABQB 143, 2000 CarswellAlta 213, 260 A.R.
245, Lee J. said, at p.
254: Rule 214(4) relates to read ins.
Its purpose is to allow the witness to add to half an answer, or to clarify a passage which has been taken out of context or otherwise is misleading.
The same principle can and should be applied to a situation such as the present one where a part of the examination for discovery has been put to a party in cross-examination.
Meaning of “if it is so connected” in old R.
214(4) (current R.

214(4) permits the extra read-in “… if it is so connected with the part so used that the first mentioned part ought not be used without the other part.” It is, therefore, incumbent upon the [party invoking the rule] to demonstrate this connection and for me to ask what is meant by “if it is so connected” and “ought” not to be used… Our own Court of Appeal in Rogers v.
L.R.
28], considered the meaning of the words “connected with” and “ought not to be used.” Mr.
Justice of Appeal Beck defined one in terms of the other; and said [p.

178]: The present Rule entitles the party, part of whose examination is being used by the opposite party, to have any further part put which ‘ought’ to be put in, that is to say, as said by Cotton, L.J., in Lyell v.
Kennedy (1884), 27 Ch.
D.
1 at p.
15 …‘which is fairly connected with’ the part proffered—‘connected in sense or substance.’Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v.
Stearns Catalytic Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 337 (Q.B.), at 341-42, per MacCallum J.
In Edmonton (City) v.
Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc., 2000 ABQB 265, 2000 CarswellAlta 393, 265 A.R.
285, Lee J., at p.
287, said: The test for letting the party or parties opposite supplement or augment the read-in in any particular instance is “connectedness” with the part being read-in.
In my previous Reasons in this action in regard to the scope of cross and reexamination [(2000), 260 A.R.
245 (Q.B.)], I indicated that “connectedness” does not always require “adjacency”.

His Lordship was referring to the fact that in his previous Reasons he had permitted opposing counsel to make reference to a portion of the transcript which was more than 100 pages away from the segment being used by examining counsel.
As long as the portions were “connected”, they need not be “adjacent” to each other in the transcript.
In 155569 Canada Ltd. v.
248524 Alberta Ltd.
90 (Q.B.), Veit J. said, at p.
92: …[T]he proper test for the assessment of the completeness of a proposed read-in was fairness to the party based on the specific question asked rather than on the topic addressed in the questions.

In other words, the objective was not to require the opposing party to read-in everything the examined party said on a topic, but to ensure that the whole answer the party examined gave to a question was read-in.
Use of Employee and Representative Transcripts Together In Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v.
Stearns Catalytic Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 337 (Q.B.), MacCallum J. was presiding at a trial in which the plaintiff was reading in from discovery certain questions and answers given by a Mr.
Sambell, an employee of the defendant.
The defendant applied, pursuant to R.
214(4), for the court to use part of the discovery transcript of the defendant's representative, a Mr.
Phannenstiel.
In the words of MacCallum J., the read-ins from Mr.
Sambell were “not being read in directly, but rather through the defendant's representative Phannenstiel as information of the defendant”.
For an explanation of that process, see “Use of Examinations of Employees”, infra.

After the read-ins by the Plaintiff, “the defendants rose to apply to use not another part of the same examination of Sambell, but rather Phannenstiel's responses to the … generic question in which he said in effect that he indeed had information which was contrary or inconsistent with Sambell's evidence”.
Should the defendants be permitted to use that evidence pursuant to R.
At pp.

340-41, his Lordship said: Nobody argues, I suppose, that a party could demand that B's discovery answers be read in to clarify something in A's discovery answers; but we are not here dealing with A and B.
We are dealing with only A, Stearns Catalytic.
I am simply not listening to the answers of Sambell being read in as his answers.
Notionally, I am listening to the information of the defendant Stearns Catalytic.
Were it otherwise, Sambell's answers as I pointed out above could not be read in.
So here is what the plaintiffs propose.

Although the defendant's officer has responded affirmatively to the … generic question and has provided the particulars required, the plaintiffs may use these responses for informational purposes; but the defendants are precluded from using particulars of the responses by way of explanation or clarification under R.
To me, this is unfair.
To again emphasize the notional aspect of this situation, the person whose evidence was read in by the plaintiffs is Stearns Catalytic.

This point was made repeatedly by the plaintiffs in support of their argument made earlier in this trial that read-ins such as they have made on October the 19th are not hearsay and are within the purview of the rules which do not authorize the use at trial of discovery answers of employees, per se.
That covers I think the objection that the examination of a different person is being used to clarify the read-in.
MacCallum J. then discussed other aspects of the application.
He concluded by saying, at p.
342: The plaintiffs have expressed concern that they might be bound by the additional read-ins as part of their case.
They need not be.

Anything extra which might be read in at the defendant's request simply becomes evidence in the case generally to be judged by the ordinary Rules of Evidence and to be accorded the weight which it merits.
